structured_extraction.program_name: City-Wide Affordable Housing Tax Increment Financing (TIF)
structured_extraction.program_description: A citywide public financing tool and tax increment financing program designed to help eliminate vacant housing in Baltimore by generating funds to fix up dangerous structures, convert them to community green space, support the redevelopment of vacant properties for affordable housing, and deliver public infrastructure improvements. The program targets vacant properties in the City-Wide Affordable Housing TIF District established by Baltimore City Council in December 2024, making it the first large-scale non-contiguous TIF implemented by a major U.S. city. The district includes approximately 4,000 formerly vacant buildings that have been redeveloped and now occupied, and approximately 4,000 vacant properties that have been issued a Vacant Building Notice. TIF funds are provided as reimbursement grants to reduce appraisal gaps and support either public infrastructure for new housing construction or construction costs to redevelop vacant buildings into occupied homes. Funds can be used for hard construction costs to rehabilitate vacant buildings into rental or ownership housing, for constructing public infrastructure for city-sponsored homeownership projects, public infrastructure improvements like sidewalks and parks, and homeowner grants to help residents qualify for newly rehabbed homes. The program has approximately $15-18 million available for redevelopment with an estimated $3 million allocated to legacy residents, current TIF District residents, and small/emerging developers for privately-owned properties, with initial bond issuance approved for $65 million and $150 million in total TIF bonds planned to transform approximately 3,900 housing units. Applicants source their own funds and receive reimbursement through a process involving third-party inspector approval, cost verification, and submission of reimbursement requests. The program prioritizes legacy residents, small and emerging developers, and women and minority-owned businesses.
list_of_eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: TIF reimbursement grants for hard construction costs on eligible vacant properties. Applicants source their own funds to complete work and then submit requests for reimbursement based on review and approval by a third-party inspector, verification that costs match actual construction expenses, and approval of a Request for Reimbursement. The average award is anticipated to be around $50,000 and will vary based on property size, condition, end use (rental or homeownership), level of affordability, and the appraisal gap. Funds are provided to bridge appraisal gaps where renovation costs exceed the resale value and to fill project financing gaps. Reimbursement options include: one request when the project is complete and has received a Use and Occupancy Permit, or through a draw schedule with one or two draws totaling up to 90 percent of approved construction costs, one draw when the property receives its Use and Occupancy Permit, and one draw when the property is occupied. Tax Increment Financing bonds capture future property tax revenue increases to fund vacant housing rehabilitation or conversion to community green space. The district authorizes $65 million in TIF bonds initially, with a planned $150 million expected over the life of the project. Estimated $15-18 million available for this funding round with approximately $3 million allocated to legacy residents, current TIF District residents, and small/emerging developers for privately-owned properties. Funding is used to provide reimbursement for hard construction costs only, deliver public infrastructure including sidewalks, parks, alleys, and address home appraisal gaps. The Department of Finance expects to begin deploying funding from the first tranche of TIF bonds in the second half of 2025. TIF bonds are repaid from increases in property tax assessments and property tax revenues generated in the district. Award amounts are determined by various factors including project description, budget, schedule, financing, ability to complete projects, obtain a Use and Occupancy Permit, application scoring, available funds, and affordability levels (60%, 80%, or up to 115% of area median income). Awardees execute a grant agreement with DHCD.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: October 3, 2025 (first round); multiple rounds anticipated with dates to be determined. The initial application period for prior rounds is now closed.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit organizations, for-profit developers, limited liability companies (LLCs), individual residents, property owners, developers, legacy residents, small and emerging developers, women-owned businesses, and minority-owned businesses seeking to rehabilitate vacant properties into affordable housing or purchase newly rehabbed homes. Homeowners and prospective homeowners earning up to 115 percent of area median income (approximately $149,845 for a household of four as of 2025), prioritized at 60% and 80% of area median income. Residents can occupy properties if annual household income does not exceed 115 percent of area median income. Rental tenants must meet the same income requirement. Licensed contractors must be licensed at time of project execution.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Hard construction costs only including roofs, framing, flooring, electrical, HVAC, plumbing, site improvements, building structure, foundations, interior and exterior finishes, building service systems (electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilation, air-conditioning), alarm systems, elevators, fire protection systems, telecommunications cabling, doors, windows, and porch repair. Public infrastructure to support new housing construction including streets, curbs, gutters, sidewalks, lighting, landscaping, roads, water and utilities. Funds can also be used for renovation and rehabilitation of vacant housing units, conversion to community green space, construction of public infrastructure required to build new housing as part of city-sponsored homeownership development projects, public infrastructure improvements such as sidewalks, parks, and alleys, homeowner grants to help residents qualify for newly rehabbed homes, and addressing home appraisal gaps. TIF funds cannot be used for soft costs like architectural and engineering services, site development and civil work, excavation, landscaping, city utilities, permitting costs, financing costs such as interest, community amenities, work on occupied properties, or to reimburse work that has already been completed. Hard costs must be capitalized into project costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Properties must be located in the City-Wide Affordable Housing TIF District as established by City Council Bill 24-0595 (Ordinance 24-443) and approved by Baltimore City Council in December 2024. The district includes approximately 4,000 formerly vacant buildings that have been redeveloped and now occupied, and approximately 4,000 vacant properties that have been issued a Vacant Building Notice. There are 3,991 vacant properties identified in the TIF legislation that could qualify for TIF funds. The district covers nearly 4,000 properties in specific neighborhoods across Baltimore including Broadway East, Harlem Park, Druid Heights, Park Heights, Upton, East Baltimore Midway, and Coldstream Homestead Montebello. Available throughout Baltimore City, including vacant properties in East and West Baltimore neighborhoods. Applicants can use the Baltimore Affordable Housing TIF property locator application to determine if a specific property is eligible, marked with a green dot if eligible for TIF funds.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Properties included in the TIF legislation are eligible to receive TIF funds. Some properties are already part of established development projects or will be included as part of a Request for Proposals/Qualifications. Each bond series will include properties available through an open application process. Applicants complete a full application using the Neighborly Platform (https://portal.neighborlysoftware.com/baltimoremd/Participant), available beginning September 19. Complete a funding application available on DHCD's website and provide information including property details, budgets, proof of site control, evidence of organizational capacity, and financial statements. Construction budgets are reviewed by the City's Bond Counsel to confirm eligible use of TIF Bond proceeds. Applications for privately owned properties are evaluated for threshold requirements and then scored. Applications from Developer Registry members or those with a Linked Development Agreement are evaluated only on threshold requirements and will not be scored as they were previously approved through a competitive process. Award amounts are determined based on project description, budget, schedule, financing, and ability to complete projects. Applicants who are awarded funds will receive an Award Letter specifying the amount of TIF funds and eligible properties. Before a Grant Agreement can be executed, applicants must provide evidence of ownership such as a copy of the title or information from the State Department of Assessments and Taxation website. Once a Grant Agreement is executed, grantees must complete construction, obtain inspections by a third-party inspector, submit requests for reimbursement with documentation of actual costs and third-party approval, and ensure the property receives a Use and Occupancy permit and is occupied within 12 months. Interested parties should check back for available properties and submit applications according to the application timeline for each bond series.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Catalyst Grants (CCG) Round 6 Operating Funds
structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant program supported by the City of Baltimore that provides funding to neighborhood-based partner organizations in historically disinvested areas. Established in 2018 by the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD), the program supports locally driven community development work, neighborhood-based revitalization initiatives, and neighborhood revitalization and transformation efforts. Through competitive funding rounds, the program awards operating funds to help make neighborhoods stronger. The program values neighborhoods, promotes equity and community development, and provides flexible funding for organizational priorities including staffing, consultants, equipment, community organizing, and other operational needs.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to $1,020,000 in operating funds available through this competitive awards program. Emerging Organizations receive $120,000 each (6 awards available) and Established Organizations receive $60,000 each (5 awards available). Award amounts are determined by the Housing Commissioner; DHCD reserves the right to award different amounts than requested and is subject to final underwriting and City Board of Estimates approval. Funds must be spent within 12 months of executing the Funding Agreement with the Board of Estimates, with a spending deadline of June 30, 2027. Operating funds support the ongoing costs of organizations doing community-driven revitalization work and community projects that strengthen neighborhoods, including staffing, consultants, equipment, and community organizing. New application opportunities are announced at different times.

Organizations without 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(6) status may apply through eligible Partner Applicant or Fiscal Agent arrangements. structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Operating funds and project funding to support locally driven community development work, neighborhood-based revitalization initiatives, neighborhood revitalization and transformation efforts, and community projects that strengthen neighborhoods. structured_extraction.program_name: Community Land Trusts - Homeownership and Rental NOFAs (2022 Round)
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Department of Housing & Community Development issued two Notices of Funding Availability for the Affordable Housing Trust Fund Community Land Trusts Program. The City seeks to promote equitable community development by directing funds to communities suffering from historical disinvestment. Projects support community development goals of meeting demand for affordable housing and integrating land trust housing as part of a broader mixed-income housing strategy. Two separate NOFAs make up to $1.5 million available for rental projects and up to $4.0 million available for homeownership projects, supporting both new construction and preservation of existing rentals, as well as perpetually affordable homeownership through shared equity models where the land trust owns the land and purchasers build equity as property values grow. Seeks impactful projects that leverage additional investment and demonstrate local residents and stakeholders leading revitalization efforts.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Two separate NOFAs provide funding from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund: (1) Up to $1.5 million available for rental projects, with up to $750,000 per project to support new construction and/or preservation of existing rentals. Maximum per unit: $20,000 (fewer than 10 units) or $50,000 (10+ units) for 50% AMI households; $100,000 (fewer than 10 units) or $120,000 (10+ units) for 30% AMI households. Funds can support up to 50% of Total Development Cost (TDC) for units at 50% AMI or up to 66% TDC for units at 30% AMI. (2) Up to $4.0 million available for homeownership projects, with up to $1,000,000 per project. Maximum per unit: $50,000 for units at ≤50% AMI; $100,000 per unit for ≤30% AMI. Funds can support up to 50% of TDC for 50% AMI units or 66% of TDC for 30% AMI units. Up to 25% advancement for predevelopment/acquisition costs and up to 20% of award for operating costs directly related to project implementation. Qualified applicants working in multiple communities can submit more than one project without penalty. Funds support site acquisition, personnel and consultants, construction and rehabilitation, sustainability features, local hiring and apprenticeships, development activities, appraisals, market feasibility studies, environmental assessments, and project implementation on a reimbursement basis.

structured_extraction.program_audience: Community Land Trusts seeking to develop affordable rental and homeownership projects in Baltimore City. Applicants must be CLTs organized or managed by nonprofit organizations exempt from taxation under §501(c)(2), (3), or (4) of the Internal Revenue Code and registered as Affordable Housing Land Trusts with Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation. CLTs must partner with an experienced developer (who has completed at least 5 development projects). Multiple land trusts can submit collaborative or joint applications. Projects serve low and very-low income households earning 50% or less of Area Median Income, with at least half of available funds serving households at 30% AMI. Program also supports single mothers seeking affordable rental housing and veterans.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Support for Community Land Trust rental and homeownership projects providing affordable housing to low and very-low income households. Eligible uses include site acquisition and development; personnel and consultants; construction and rehabilitation; sustainability features; local hiring and apprenticeships; development activities; appraisals; market feasibility studies; environmental assessments; predevelopment and acquisition costs; operating costs directly related to project implementation; architecture and engineering; administration; marketing and sales; builder profit, overhead, and construction management; and related project costs.

Preference for opportunity areas to create affordability in high-cost areas. Projects should not concentrate only in already heavily subsidized housing areas. Projects must demonstrate consistency with community or neighborhood plans and address neighborhood revitalization and blight elimination.

structured_extraction.program_description: A comprehensive community cleanup program offered by Baltimore City DPW that supports cleanup events of all sizes. structured_extraction.program_description: The Continuum of Care program, funded annually by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, is a competitive federal funding program that promotes a community-wide commitment to ending homelessness by providing grants to nonprofit providers and state and local governments to quickly rehouse individuals and families experiencing homelessness while minimizing trauma and dislocation. The program aims to make homelessness rare and brief, create systems to help homeless people access services, use Housing First approach, help homeless people access benefits and employment, ensure fair treatment, and use data to determine which programs work best. More than 75% of funds support programs that provide both homes and support services to people who have experienced long-term homelessness, with a significant portion directed to Permanent Supportive Housing that combines long-term housing subsidies with supportive services. Federal funding supports rapid rehousing, prevention services, temporary shelter, supportive housing, emergency shelter, transitional housing, permanent housing, supportive services only, Street Outreach, and Homeless Management Information Systems (HMIS). Service providers can apply for new projects, expansion projects, renewal projects, or Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program (YHDP) projects through a local competitive Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) process, with projects ranked and selected for inclusion in the Continuum of Care's consolidated application to HUD.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: HUD provides annual grants to nonprofit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations and government entities through a competitive local and national Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) process. FY 2025 total funding: $42,797,644 including Annual Renewal Demand ($31,796,073), Bonus Project Funding ($6,359,215), Domestic Violence Bonus Funding ($3,142,356), and CoC Planning Grant Funds ($1,500,000). More than 75% of funds support programs that provide both homes and support services to people who have experienced long-term homelessness. Permanent housing subject to 30% funding cap. The program funds three main types of projects: permanent housing, supportive services only, and Homeless Management Information Systems (HMIS). In Baltimore City, more than 75 percent of CoC funding is directed to Permanent Supportive Housing programs, which combine long-term housing subsidies with supportive services. Project types include Permanent Housing-Permanent Supportive Housing (PH-PSH), Permanent Housing-Rapid Rehousing (PH-RRH), Joint Transitional Housing/Permanent Housing-Rapid Rehousing (Joint TH/PH-RRH), Transitional Housing (TH), Supportive Services Only (SSO), Supportive Services Only-Coordinated Entry (SSO-CE), Safe Haven (SH), Street Outreach (SO), and HMIS. Applicants select appropriate application templates for New, Expansion, Renewal, or Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program (YHDP) Renewal/Replacement projects. Funding supports rapid rehousing, emergency shelter, transitional housing, supportive services, providing homes, improving the Homeless Management Information System, promoting access to mainstream applications, and optimizing self-sufficiency among those experiencing homelessness. Applicants must provide minimum 25% match (cash or in-kind, excluding leasing costs). Specific funding amounts and project terms determined through competitive process. Applications submitted through Neighborly portal or via email. Local areas have approximately 60 to 75 days to apply.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: FY 2025: Friday, December 12, 2025, at 5:00 pm EST. FY 2024: Wednesday, September 25, 2024, at 5:00 pm EST. Varies annually; local areas have approximately 60 to 75 days to apply.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations and government agencies serving individuals and families experiencing homelessness or at risk of homelessness in the Baltimore City Continuum of Care, including elderly individuals, physically disabled persons, substance use disorder populations, survivors of domestic violence, unaccompanied youth, survivors of sexual assault and trafficking, persons with disabilities, chronically homeless individuals, veterans, LGBTQ+ individuals and families, Black and Brown communities, persons returning from incarceration, and individuals exiting health care or residential care facilities. Organizations that have not previously received CoC funding are invited to apply.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Permanent housing, rapid rehousing, supportive housing programs, prevention services, temporary shelter, emergency shelter, transitional housing, supportive services only, Homeless Management Information Systems (HMIS), Street Outreach, Coordinated Entry operations, services that promote self-sufficiency, access to mainstream programs and benefits (Medicare, Medicaid, SSI, SNAP, TANF, Food Stamps), case management, life skills, housing costs (leasing, rental assistance, move-in assistance, deposits, security deposits up to 2 months rent, housing damage payments up to 2 months rent), trauma-informed care, substance use disorder treatment, mental health services, employment assistance, legal services, health services, workforce development, program administration and staffing (up to 10% for administrative costs), client assistance, cellular phone and service, internet costs, utility assistance and arrears (up to 6 months), rental arrears (up to 6 months), legal fees and court costs, driving fines and vehicle registration/insurance, transportation assistance, host home and kinship care model payments, moving expenses, housing start-up expenses (up to $300 per participant), landlord incentive funds, diversion programs, data collection and analysis, staff capacity, equipment and technology access, and staff training on racial equity and homelessness. Trauma minimization and dislocation prevention.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Each year, HUD announces a national funding competition through a Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA). When announced, Baltimore City holds a local competition to select both renewal and new homeless services projects that match HUD's priorities and local needs. Applicants create an account and log into the Neighborly portal to upload application materials, or may submit by email to HSPApplications@baltimorecity.gov. Applicants are encouraged to add two points of contact in Neighborly before the deadline and to participate in the Bidders Conference for guidance. Applicants select appropriate application templates for New, Expansion, Renewal, or YHDP Renewal/Replacement projects. An authorized individual at the agency uploads all documents, completes supporting and match documentation, and certifies submission. Neighborly sends an automated confirmation upon receipt. Applications are reviewed by the Resource Allocation Committee and CoC Board, with final rankings sent to board for review prior to HUD submission. The Resource Allocation Committee reviews applications, ranks projects by performance and competitiveness, and selects which projects fit HUD requirements and community needs and will be included in the consolidated CoC application submitted to HUD. HUD direct grantees submit applications directly through e-SNAPS according to HUD procedures. Public notification of ranked projects is provided prior to HUD submission.

structured_extraction.program_description: A grant program administered by Baltimore City that supports nonprofit organizations working in close partnership with communities to address the digital divide through education, outreach, planning, and implementation activities. The program funds the creation of community-led digital inclusion plans and supports projects addressing gaps in digital literacy, advanced IT skills training, and digital creative education. It helps residents gain essential digital resources and tools needed to engage in the modern digital world.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Three categories of grants are provided: (1) Education and Outreach grants ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 to fund community-based activities raising awareness of the digital divide and supporting programming to address it; (2) Planning grants up to $50,000 to support community-building efforts to develop neighborhood digital inclusion plans; and (3) Implementation grants up to $75,000 to support communities in putting digital inclusion plans into action. Additionally, three tiers of larger grants available through separate categories: Tier 1 Digital Literacy Education Training grants up to $200,000 for digital literacy education programs for older adults or tech hubs at recreation centers; Tier 2 Advanced Digital Education and IT Fundamentals Programming grants up to $200,000 for IT skills training and industry-recognized certifications; Tier 3 Digital Creatives and Virtual Makerspaces Programming grants up to $200,000 for digital creative classes and workshops including coding, digital media creation, robotics, video editing, and 3D printing.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federally funded congregate nutrition program established under the Older Americans Act that provides nutritious meals in a social dining setting for seniors in Baltimore City. The program operates at more than 50 congregate dining sites throughout the city and promotes health, reduces isolation, and offers educational events, social activities, and opportunities to make friends. Free meals (lunch or dinner) are available, with special options including Kosher and Korean meals. Participants can make confidential voluntary donations of $1.25 for regular meals or $2.00 for kosher meals to support program costs and serve more seniors.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides free nutritious meals (lunch or dinner) at more than 50 congregate dining sites throughout Baltimore City. Participants can make confidential voluntary donations of $1.25 for regular meals or $2.00 for kosher meals. The program also offers special meals including Kosher and Korean options, as well as social activities, educational seminars, health programs, volunteer opportunities, trips, speakers, group activities, special events, holiday celebrations, craft activities, parties, games, and entertainment. Registration is required.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Seniors 60 years of age or older, their spouses regardless of age, and disabled persons younger than 60 who reside in residential buildings where the program operates.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Meals must be consumed at congregate dining sites. Participants can make optional donations to support the cost of meals and allow more seniors to participate.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. There are more than 50 Eating Together sites located throughout Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Must be 60 years of age or older, OR be the spouse of an eligible participant regardless of age, OR be a disabled person younger than 60 residing in a residential building where the program operates
Must complete a registration form to participate
Must be able to attend meals at one of the congregate dining sites
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Eligible individuals must complete a registration form to join the program. Upon registration, participants receive a membership card that they swipe each time they attend a meal. Menus are posted monthly to allow participants to reserve meals for specific dates. Call 443-573-0161 or 410-396-1337 for more information and to sign up.

structured_extraction.program_description: Request for Proposal to provide emergency shelter services for persons experiencing homelessness within Baltimore City's Continuum of Care. The program funds three emergency homeless shelter sites offering 24/7 dignified residential settings with day-to-day operations management, certified food services, janitorial services, shelter monitoring, case management, complaint response/monitoring, data collection, linkage to community support, and supportive services to help people experiencing homelessness transition to housing stability and self-sufficiency.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grant funding for operating emergency homeless shelter sites. Funding supports: shelter facility operations (24/7 beds including overflow capacity), meal provision (twice daily, 365 days/year), case management services (minimum twice monthly per client), certified food services, janitorial services, shelter monitoring and security staff, fire safety compliance, pest management, HMIS data collection, staff salaries and training, and supportive services. Three shelter sites available: city-owned facility at 620 Fallsway serving single men (175 beds) and single women (75 beds) with overflow capacity (15 beds each); city-owned facility at 1200 N. Fremont Ave. serving single women (70 beds) and families (8 beds) with overflow capacity; and a privately-owned facility serving families (150 beds). Performance period was July 1, 2020 through June 30, 2021. Funding comes from federal, state, and local appropriations and is subject to applicable laws and funding source regulations.

Payments can be applied toward arrearages for the most recent three-month period. The City has designated $2,000,000 for the program, estimated to support 100 to 300 households.

structured_extraction.program_description: A grant program that provides funding to organizations to deliver free transportation services to individuals and families experiencing homelessness within Baltimore City. Services connect homeless individuals and families to shelters and other homeless services program locations within the Baltimore Continuum of Care, with priority given based on vulnerability and severity of service needs. Transportation must be provided year-round during both winter shelter periods (October 15 through March 31) with expanded hours (5:45 am - 11:00 pm) and non-winter shelter periods (April 1 through October 14) with standard hours (5:45 am - 9:00 pm), seven days per week. Services operate with a non-discrimination approach regardless of where or how people present for services. Enhanced services are provided during Code Blue Extreme Cold Alerts. Wheelchair accessible vehicles are required.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The grant provides funding to nonprofit organizations and city agencies to operate free transportation services for homeless individuals and families. Services operate year-round with expanded hours during winter season (October 15 - March 31): winter hours 5:45 am - 11:00 pm and non-winter hours 5:45 am - 9:00 pm, seven days per week. Enhanced services provided during Code Blue Extreme Cold Alerts. Funding covers personnel costs (labor and fringe benefits), vehicle operations and maintenance, supportive and direct services, administrative fees (supplies, materials, equipment), operating costs including 2-way radios and mobile devices, vehicle procurement/leasing and fueling, insurance and liability coverage, and staff training and development. Organizations must operate 2-3 wheelchair accessible vehicles (non-Code Blue) and 4 vehicles plus 2 replacements during Code Blue. Organizations receive grants to deliver transportation based on service demand, available funds, and provider capacity.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Friday, August 16, 2019 at 5:00 pm
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit organizations and city agencies that can provide transportation services to homeless individuals and families experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City, including single adults and families. Unaccompanied youth are excluded.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding must be used to provide free transportation services to shelters and other homeless services program locations within the Baltimore Continuum of Care. Permitted uses include personnel costs (labor and fringe benefits), vehicle procurement, maintenance, and fueling, insurance and liability coverage, supportive and direct services, administrative fees and supplies (supplies, materials, equipment, 2-way radios, mobile devices, cleaning products), and staff training and development. Organizations must prioritize assistance based on the vulnerability and severity of service needs and provide non-discriminatory services regardless of where or how people present for services. Funds may not be used to support religious instruction, counseling, or proselytizing activities.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Services must be provided within Baltimore City and the Baltimore Continuum of Care (BCOC). Service locations include 8 routine shelter pick-up sites and 6 community locations. Transportation services are required during both winter shelter periods (October 15 through March 31) with expanded hours and non-winter shelter periods (April 1 through October 14) with standard hours.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federal formula grant program that provides funding for emergency shelter, transitional housing, rapid rehousing, homelessness prevention services, and supportive services for homeless individuals and families and those at risk of homelessness in Baltimore City. Implements strategic investments in three areas: Homelessness Prevention, Homeless Intervention Services, and Housing Placement, Stabilization, and Support.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal formula grant funding allocated annually to Baltimore City for emergency shelter, transitional housing, rapid rehousing assistance (up to 24 months), homelessness prevention services (including rental assistance, utility assistance, legal services, mortgage assistance), street outreach, day resource centers, respite care, and case management services. Homelessness Prevention includes direct financial assistance for eviction prevention, housing relocation services, financial counseling, landlord mediation, and legal support. Homeless Intervention Services include basic needs (food, hygiene, clothing), health/behavioral health services, mainstream benefits connection, and case management. Housing Placement uses a housing first approach with rapid rehousing and support services. Funds support the Coordinated Access and Entry System for centralized assessment of persons needing homeless services. Expected to serve approximately 200 homeless individuals or households annually through rapid rehousing and eviction prevention, shelter approximately 762 homeless persons, and provide services to approximately 1,975 homeless persons. 5-year funding allocation (2025-2029): $8,502,305.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Baltimore City applies for ESG funding through submission of a HUD-approved Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan. Subrecipient agencies are selected through an annual RFP cycle (minimum 30 days notice). Coordinated Entry system uses assessment tools including Housing Assessment, Client Unit Preference Assessment, Vulnerability Assessment, and TAY-VI-SPDAT. Priority given to chronically homeless individuals, then homeless individuals with disabling conditions, then homeless individuals without disabling conditions (prioritized by vulnerability score). Separate Victim Coordinated Entry system for domestic violence survivors through House of Ruth of Maryland. Real-time bed availability and capacity management. Monitoring consists of onsite visits, desk audits, and reviews of monthly expenditure reporting.

structured_extraction.program_description: Request for proposals from qualified non-profit organizations to operate non-congregate shelter facilities and provide supportive services for adult individuals experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City. The program funds two separate shelter projects: one serving 135 single adult men and another serving 145 single adult women. Services operate 24/7, seven days a week and include emergency shelter, food service, hygiene products, care coordination, mental health and substance use services, and behavioral health crisis management. Selected projects will receive a one-year contract from July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2023.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Funding through the City's General Funds, Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), Homelessness Solutions Program (HSP), and Department of Social Services Grant (DSS) to support non-congregate emergency shelter operations for single adult men (135 beds) and single adult women (145 beds). Selected projects will receive a one-year contract from July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2023. Funding covers 24/7 facility management, intake, recordkeeping, reporting, security, supervision, three meals and snacks daily, hygiene and sanitation products, on-site care coordination emphasizing rehousing, mental health and substance use services, behavioral health crisis management, staff salaries and training, case management, harm reduction, discharge planning, and transportation. The exact amount of available funding has not yet been confirmed. Providers may submit more than one application and be considered for multiple eligible sources of funding.

Proposals should include the completed Project Application form and Project Budget template. The application process includes Step 1: Application Completeness Review (timeliness and thoroughness of submission), Step 2: Eligibility Review, and Step 3: Project Scoring based on five weighted categories (Project Description 30%, Organizational Experience & Capacity 20%, Collaboration 20%, Project Work Plan & Budget 25%, Overall Quality). structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant program that supports non-profit organizations and government agencies providing services to individuals and families who are at-risk of homelessness, currently homeless, low-income and living with HIV or AIDS, or at risk of crises including those with behavioral health needs. Through one application, programs can be considered for multiple eligible funding sources including the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program (HSP), Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Baltimore City Department of Social Services funds, Baltimore City Opioid Restitution Fund, Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds, and Baltimore City General Funds. The program is designed to streamline the application process and support comprehensive homeless services and housing assistance. Grant term runs July 1 through June 30 of the following year. The program accepts both new and renewal project proposals. The program responds to the urgent housing crisis in Baltimore City and supports the city's commitment to preventing and ending homelessness with a mission to make homelessness rare, brief, and non-recurring in Baltimore City. Manages over $94 Million annually in CoC, HOPWA, ESG, HSP and other federal, state, and local funds.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grant funding from multiple sources including the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program (HSP), Baltimore City Department of Social Services, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Baltimore City Opioid Restitution Fund, Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds, and Baltimore City General Funds. Non-profit organizations and government agencies submit one application and can be considered for multiple eligible funding sources based on services provided. Grant term runs July 1 through June 30 of the following year. Specific award amounts and terms are determined in the competitive application process. Funding supports emergency shelter, drop-in centers, day centers, transitional housing, housing stabilization, homelessness prevention, rapid re-housing, street outreach, permanent supportive housing, case management, housing and services for people living with HIV or AIDS, comprehensive street outreach, and eviction prevention programs. Services include personnel costs, program operations, housing-related expenses, and supportive services. Eligible uses include street outreach engagement and case management, emergency shelter operations (overnight and day shelter), food and transportation assistance, hotel/motel vouchers, rental and financial assistance, and case management.

structured_extraction.program_audience: Qualified non-profit organizations and government agencies that provide services to individuals and families at risk of homelessness, currently homeless, low-income and living with HIV or AIDS, or at risk of crises including those with behavioral health needs in Baltimore City. Specifically serves individuals and families experiencing homelessness (Categories 1-4), at-risk individuals and families (Categories 1-3), unaccompanied youth under 25, families with children and youth, individuals fleeing domestic violence, individuals with behavioral health needs, individuals with mental illness and substance use disorders, people living with HIV/AIDS, vulnerable populations, and youth aging out of foster care.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Services and housing support including emergency shelter, drop-in centers, day centers, transitional housing, comprehensive street outreach, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, housing stabilization, homelessness prevention, housing and services for people with HIV/AIDS, case management, street outreach, eviction prevention programs. Eligible activities include comprehensive outreach services, street outreach (engagement, assessment, interventions, transportation, emergency health and mental health services), emergency shelter operations (24/7, daytime, winter), essential support services (case management, childcare, employment, health services, legal services, life skills), staff training and behavioral health clinical support, warming centers, rental assistance, arrears, deposits, utility assistance, moving costs, legal services, food assistance, emergency housing, interpretation services, transportation, mental health services, substance abuse treatment, oral health services, and onsite case management for youth aging out of foster care. Opioid restitution funds support 24/7 comprehensive outreach. General funds support transportation, meals, winter shelter outreach, and expanded services.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City. HOPWA funds serve the Baltimore-Towson Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area and Maryland counties. Primary focus on Baltimore City with specific shelter locations at 221 N. Gay Street, 300 N. Front Street, 101 South President Street, 1114 N. Mount Street, and 620 Fallsway.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: A Request for Proposals (RFP) is posted with a Bidder's Conference held prior to the application deadline. A Bidder's Conference was held on February 18, 2025 at 2:00 p.m. Interested applicants create an account in the Neighborly portal and designate two points of contact. Organizations submit complete application materials and budget worksheets appropriate for the service type via Neighborly portal by the deadline. An authorized individual certifies and submits the application. Neighborly sends an automated message confirming receipt. Applications are reviewed for eligibility across multiple funding sources, go through threshold and eligibility review followed by panel evaluation. Conditional awards are issued in April, with contract development in May and grant term beginning July 1. Organizations submit one application that can be considered for multiple eligible funding sources using provided CFA application templates and corresponding budget workbooks based on service category. May submit supplemental Word document aligned with Scope of Work if additional space needed.

structured_extraction.program_description: A homeownership incentive program that helps first-time homebuyers at or below 80% of the area median income by providing down payment assistance, gap funding to reduce loan balance, and interest rate buydown. The program is part of Baltimore City's broader homeownership initiatives designed to make homeownership more affordable and accessible by lowering closing costs and boosting down payments.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides 50% of the required down payment, gap funding (calculated as the difference between 30% of annual household income and annual mortgage payment) to reduce the loan balance, and an interest rate buydown of up to 2.5% of sales price. An additional $5,000 bonus may be available for: (a) purchase of a previously rented and occupied home (6+ months), or (b) buyer or household member with a disability. Up to 50% of closing costs may also be covered. Most funds are provided as forgivable loans that do not need to be repaid if the borrower stays in the home for five years. Funding is provided annually based on the City's fiscal calendar (July 1 to June 30) on a first-come, first-served basis until exhausted. Funds cannot be used for realtor fees and recipients cannot receive cash at settlement table. Not available if receiving Maryland Mortgage Program funds.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Funding is provided annually based on the City's fiscal calendar (July 1 to June 30). Applications are accepted on a first-come, first-served basis until funding is exhausted.
structured_extraction.program_audience: First-time homebuyers at or below 80% of the area median income who are purchasing homes in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funds can be used for down payment assistance, principal reduction on loan balance, interest rate buydowns, and up to 50% of closing costs on home purchase loans. Cannot be used for realtor fees.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Limited to Baltimore City. Recipients must purchase a home within Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Must be a first-time homebuyer
Household income must be at or below 80% of the area median income
Must complete homeownership counseling from a City-approved homeownership counseling agency within one year before purchasing
Must contribute at least $1,000 of own money towards the home purchase
Housing counselor and lender must complete the online application
Must have a settlement date at least 30 days after submitting application
Cannot receive cash at settlement table
Cannot be receiving Maryland Mortgage Program funds (for interest rate buydown eligibility)
Income verification required
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Attend a Live Baltimore Trolley Tour. Access the online calculator at dhcd.baltimorecity.gov/hho/homeownership-incentives to determine eligibility and funding amount. Sign in to the Applicant Portal at portal.neighborlysoftware.com/baltimoremd/Participant using Google Chrome or other modern browsers (Internet Explorer v10+, Firefox, Safari). Register an account with email address and password, validate email ownership via validation link sent to your email. Login with registered email and password. Submit an application. Your housing counselor and lender must complete the online application. Provide the Title Company's Employer Identification Number (EIN) under H. Closing Information. Processing typically takes 10 to 15 business days after approval. Note: System automatically logs out after 30 minutes of inactivity. Password reset available via 'Forgot your Password?' link.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federal formula grant program that provides funding to build homes and apartments for rent or purchase, helping create safe, affordable housing in Baltimore City. The program supports housing development and preservation activities through annual federal formula grant allocations to Baltimore City as outlined in the City's Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan. The program funds construction and rehabilitation of housing to create affordable rental units for low-income households, supports acquisition, homebuyer assistance, homeowner rehabilitation, multifamily rental new construction and rehabilitation, new construction for ownership, and tenant-based rental assistance. Uses federal funds to leverage state, local, foundation, and private financing to create decent and affordable housing, suitable living environment, and economic opportunity.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal formula grant funding allocated annually to Baltimore City through the Office of Project Finance to support the construction, development, and preservation of rental and purchase-ready affordable housing. In PY 2025, the program funds eligible rental projects only and will not fund homeownership activities or tenant-based rental assistance. Expected outcomes include approximately 321 new rental units, 5 rehabilitated rental units, 11 new homebuyer units, assistance to 200 first-time homebuyer households, 3,590 households completing homeownership counseling, emergency repairs for 412 households, lead remediation for 185 households, and 617 households receiving HOPWA tenant-based rental assistance. Funds support new rental unit construction, rehabilitation of existing units, homebuyer down payment assistance, emergency repairs, lead hazard remediation, homeownership counseling, rapid rehousing, rental assistance subsidies, and housing development and acquisition. Direct subsidies provided for HOME-assisted homebuyers with recapture provisions based on years occupied during affordability period.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Bi-annual Notices of Funding Availability (NOFA) published on DHCD website
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low- to moderate-income households, extremely low-income households (0-30% AMI), very low-income households (30-50% AMI), low-income households (50-80% AMI), first-time homebuyers, families with children, elderly residents (62+ years old), persons with disabilities, large families, single-person households, victims of domestic violence, formerly homeless individuals and families, persons living with HIV/AIDS, public housing residents, homeless persons and those at risk of homelessness, unaccompanied youth, veterans and their families, chronically homeless individuals, and legacy residents. The program serves renters and homeowners in Baltimore City with special focus on low- and moderate-income families earning at or below 120% of Area Median Income, legacy residents earning 60% of AMI, and special needs populations.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Construction, development, and preservation of affordable rental and owner-occupied housing; acquisition of properties; homebuyer down payment assistance; homeowner housing rehabilitation and critical repairs; tenant-based rental assistance; new multifamily rental construction and rehabilitation; emergency repairs and aging-in-place modifications; lead hazard remediation; homeownership counseling; housing navigation; rental assistance for homeless prevention; short-term rent, mortgage, and utility assistance; reduction of vacant and abandoned properties; property infrastructure improvements; housing stabilization services; rapid rehousing programs; and eviction prevention.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City. Priority investment in Vacancy Reduction Priority Geographies (VRPGs) including 7 Impact Investment Areas, 10 neighborhoods, and 11 strategic geographies. Programs address neighborhoods with history of disinvestment (Typology areas I and J that overlay past redlining areas). Activities also prioritize Asset Building Neighborhoods (census tracts A-B, I-J) and Middle Market Neighborhoods (census tracts C-H). Geographic targeting emphasizes whole-block outcomes addressing every vacant property and lot on a block. HOPWA funds allocated to Anne Arundel, Baltimore, Carroll, Harford, Howard, and Queen Anne's Counties.

structured_extraction.program_description: House Baltimore is a collaboration between property owners and managers, community members, and homeless service providers that helps property owners run successful rental properties while providing housing to people experiencing homelessness. The program offers financial incentives, support services, and a dedicated listing platform to connect property owners with tenants exiting homelessness. It is part of Baltimore City's broader Housing Navigation and Landlord Recruitment Support initiative, which was launched in 2023 with $7.6 million in funding to provide housing navigation services to individuals experiencing homelessness and landlord recruitment and engagement support.
list_of_eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Property owners receive a $2,000 incentive payment for each new lease agreement, guaranteed for the first five units leased with possibility for additional incentives if flexible screening criteria are offered. Property owners can file claims for damage and vacancy reimbursement up to $5,000 per unit for expenses caused by tenants. The program also provides access to a free listing platform (Padmission), housing specialist support, and wraparound services from local homeless services agencies. The program is supported by $7.6 million in funding to provide housing navigation services and landlord recruitment and engagement support.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Property owners and managers in Baltimore City interested in leasing units to people exiting homelessness, and individuals experiencing homelessness seeking housing
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Financial assistance can be used by property owners to cover lease incentive payments and reimbursement for damage and vacancy expenses caused by tenants. Funds also support housing navigation services and landlord recruitment efforts.

Unit must meet client needs as verified by service providers
Individuals must be experiencing homelessness
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the House Baltimore Interest Form. Receive orientation from the House Baltimore support team. Execute lease agreement once unit is verified to meet client needs. Confirm move-in date with client and service provider. Receive ongoing support from House Baltimore housing specialists and service providers.

structured_extraction.program_description: A joint effort funded through the American Rescue Plan Act to create permanent supportive housing and develop affordable housing units for individuals and families experiencing homelessness, at-risk of homelessness, or in vulnerable positions in Baltimore City. The program combines affordable housing, health care, and supportive services, following the Housing First model with referrals through the Coordinated Access System. The initiative commits nearly $30 million total in American Rescue Plan Act funds, including $15.2 million from the City's State and Local Recovery funds and $14.7 million from the Home Investment Partnerships Program American Rescue Plan Act funds. Up to $16 million is available from the Housing Accelerator Fund and up to $15 million from HOME-ARP. Projects are eligible for maximum awards of up to $250,000 per unit for permanent supportive housing construction, up to $100,000 per unit for traditional affordable housing construction, and up to $500,000 for predevelopment costs associated with funded units.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program commits approximately $30 million total in American Rescue Plan Act funds, including up to $15 million in HOME-ARP funding and up to $16 million from the Housing Accelerator Fund, with an additional $15.2 million from the City's State and Local Recovery funds. HAF funds available for hard and soft costs including architectural and engineering, environmental assessment, market analysis, carrying costs, zoning analysis, staff time, development consultants, and legal fees. HOME-ARP funds available for hard construction costs only. Grants and loans support construction and development of permanent supportive housing and affordable housing units that combine affordable housing, health care, and supportive services. Funds can support acquisition of privately owned property, closing financing gaps, securing set-asides of supportive housing units, and providing pre-development financing for individuals and families experiencing homelessness or housing instability. Maximum awards up to $250,000 per unit for permanent supportive housing construction, up to $100,000 per unit for traditional affordable housing construction, and up to $500,000 for predevelopment costs associated with funded units.

structured_extraction.program_name: Housing Opportunities for Persons with HIV/AIDS (HOPWA) Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A federal formula grant program providing housing assistance and supportive services for persons living with HIV/AIDS and their families in the Baltimore-Towson Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area. HOPWA supports safe and sanitary housing, stable living environments, and comprehensive supportive services necessary to maintain housing stability, gain better access to care, and enhance quality of life. The program provides tenant-based or project-based rental assistance, facility conversion and repair, new construction, short-term emergency payments for rent/mortgage/utilities, permanent housing placement, employment and education services, personal assistance, benefits access support, and referrals for treatment, childcare, nutrition, intensive care, and health services. Annual allocations are determined based on HIV case data provided by the Maryland Department of Health. Approximately 617 households receive tenant-based rental assistance annually, with 25 units in permanent housing facilities and additional support for emergency rent, mortgage, and utility assistance.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal formula grant funding allocated annually to the Baltimore-Towson Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area for housing and supportive services. HOPWA provides housing assistance including tenant-based and project-based rental assistance, facility conversion and repair, new construction, and short-term emergency payments for rent, mortgage, and utilities to prevent homelessness. Supportive services include permanent housing placement, employment and education services, personal assistance, assistance gaining access to local, state, and federal benefits and services, and resources and referrals for drug and alcohol abuse treatment and counseling, daycare, nutritional services, intensive care, and physical and mental health services. Move-in expenses such as security deposits and basic furnishings, transportation assistance, housing-focused case management, and supportive services staff salaries are also supported. All counties and cities in the Baltimore-Towson EMSA except Carroll County offer housing assistance through tenant-based rental assistance. Approximately 617 households receive tenant-based rental assistance annually.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Minimum of 30 days
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low-income persons at or below 80 percent of area median income who are medically diagnosed with HIV/AIDS and their families in the Baltimore-Towson Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area, as well as Baltimore City government and organizations serving people with HIV/AIDS. Most households qualify at or below 30% of area median income.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Housing assistance including tenant-based and project-based rental assistance, facility conversion and repair, new construction, and emergency payments for rent, mortgage, and utilities; supportive services including housing placement, employment and education services, personal assistance, benefits access assistance, and referrals for treatment, childcare, nutrition, intensive care, and health services; move-in expenses such as security deposits and basic furnishings; transportation assistance; housing-focused case management; and supportive services staff salaries.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: The program serves the Baltimore-Towson Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area (EMSA), which includes Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Anne Arundel County, Carroll County, Harford County, Howard County, and Queen Anne's County. Baltimore City is the HOPWA grantee. All counties and cities except Carroll County provide housing assistance through tenant-based rental assistance. As of June 30, 2024, the EMSA has 17,621 individuals living with HIV, with 9,805 Baltimore City residents living with HIV.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Organizations apply for HOPWA funding through a Request for Proposal (RFP) process via the Consolidated Funding Application (CFA), with a minimum of 30 days for the RFP open period. Applications undergo a two-step threshold review for eligibility and completeness, followed by competitive scoring by a review panel including MOHS staff, Continuum of Care members, Resource Allocation Committee, Lived Experience Advisory Committee, and Youth Action Board. Renewal projects are evaluated on prior-year performance and compliance. Individual applicants can contact the HOPWA Program through Coordinated Access or program providers in the Baltimore-Towson EMSA. The City of Baltimore contracts with localities within the EMSA for each jurisdiction to address the housing needs of persons living with HIV/AIDS in their communities. A Virtual Bidder's Conference is held after RFP release.

structured_extraction.program_description: A local policy that requires developers of multifamily, market-rate residential projects receiving major public subsidies or significant land use authorization to make affordable housing units available to households with limited incomes at reduced rents for 30 years. The program establishes requirements for affordable housing unit creation, tenant eligibility, leasing, and ongoing management. Units must be created at 50% and 60% of area median income (AMI) levels, with 5% of units at each level.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Developers of qualifying residential projects must provide inclusionary units equal to 10% of total dwelling units (5% affordable to households earning 50% AMI and 5% affordable to households earning 60% AMI). Inclusionary units must match market-rate unit design, exterior appearance, bedroom count, and construction quality. Units cannot be concentrated on specific floors or buildings and must offer the same amenities as market-rate units. Tenants pay the maximum affordable rent established by HUD. Units must remain affordable for 30 years from Certificate of Occupancy issuance. The city provides a High-Performance Inclusionary Housing Tax Credit to cover the difference between market rate and affordable rent.

Eligible tenants include low-income and very low-income households.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Creation and maintenance of affordable rental housing units within market-rate residential projects for low-income and very low-income households.

structured_extraction.program_description: The City of Baltimore provides capital investments (loans) to City agencies and quasi-City agencies for one-time investments in innovative projects that lead to improved results, increased revenue, and reduced operating costs for City services. The fund is designed to be self-sustaining, with savings or revenue from investments returned to the fund to support other projects. Since inception, the fund has loaned $4.88 million across 11 projects.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The Innovation Fund provides loans to Baltimore City agencies and quasi-City agencies for capital investments in systems, technology, infrastructure, and other one-time projects that generate savings or revenue. Agencies submit detailed project proposals including budget estimate, evaluation plan with measurements, implementation timeline, business case with repayment plan, risk identification and mitigation strategy, success metrics and performance measures, equity impact analysis, and specific itemized costs and financial plan. Proposals are evaluated by a review team from BBMR, CitiStatSMART, BCIT, and the Mayor's Office using a rating sheet with 8 criteria. Proposals submitted during the annual budget process may be included in the annual budget; those submitted later are assessed on a rolling basis. Loans are repaid from the financial benefits generated by the projects.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: One-time agency investments in technology, systems, infrastructure, and other capital projects that lead to improved results, increased revenue, or reduced operating costs for City services. Innovation projects with returns via new revenue, cost savings, or both. Projects may utilize human, social, organizational, physical, or technological resources.

structured_extraction.program_description: LIGHT is a single point of access for services from Baltimore's Department of Housing and Community Development's Housing Preservation Division. It provides access to three grant and loan programs plus evaluation for 60+ additional public and nonprofit programs and benefits. LIGHT helps people in Baltimore City get free or low-cost services to make their homes safer, healthier, and more comfortable through home repairs, lead hazard reduction, energy efficiency improvements, and assistance addressing high water bills and other housing-related problems. LIGHT Coordinators work with residents to identify needs and connect them with available programs and resources through case management to help coordinate eligible services.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: LIGHT provides free or low-cost services including grants, forgivable loans, and deferred loans. Forgivable loans are forgiven after 5 years if applicant lives in home as primary residence during that time and involve a lien on the home. Deferred loans are due when the home is sold and paid from sale proceeds and involve a lien on the home. Services include home repairs, fixing or replacing roofs, heating, plumbing, and electrical systems, making homes more energy-efficient, reducing lead hazards, making homes easier to access for people with disabilities, and addressing high water bills and other housing-related problems. Assistance is available through housing counselors and Community Action Centers as well as direct application.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Owner-occupied properties, eligible renters (for lead remediation), households with pregnant women or children under 6 years old (for lead remediation), and people with disabilities (for accessibility modifications) in Baltimore City who need help making their homes safer, healthier, and more comfortable.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Climatization and energy efficiency improvements, lead risk reduction remediation, home rehabilitation for emergency repairs and code violations, including attic insulation, air sealing, weatherstripping, HVAC maintenance, pipe wrapping, door and window treatment, lead paint remediation, roof repair, water and sewer duct repair, water heater replacement, electrical repair, accessibility modifications, and pipe repair. Also addresses high water bills and other housing-related problems.

structured_extraction.program_description: An anti-displacement initiative and $2 million pilot program designed to assist older adults with homeownership and housing preservation in Baltimore City. The program eliminates property tax debt for eligible legacy residents who are 65 or older, have owned their home for more than 10 years, and meet income requirements (annual household income below $73,000 for the 2025 tax year). Qualifying homeowners have their tax bills cleared in the following year through the Tax Sale Coordination and Prevention Services program, provided they enroll in the Tax Sale Deferral Program by April 15, 2026, complete financial literacy courses, and enroll in payment plans for future bills. Eligible homeowners are automatically reviewed for the program if they enroll in the Tax Sale Deferral Program. In-person application assistance is available through DHCD and the Mayor's Office of Older Adult Affairs & Advocacy.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: A $2 million pilot program providing relief through property tax debt forgiveness for qualified homeowners. Each applicant's tax lien amount is subtracted from the total $2 million pool, and the program closes once funding is exhausted (first-come first-served through April 15, 2026, while funding allows). Eligible legacy homeowners have their tax debt eliminated through one-time tax lien forgiveness from the total Fiscal Year 2027 budget, provided they enroll in the Tax Sale Deferral Program by April 15, 2026, complete financial literacy courses, and enroll in payment plans for future bills. Applications are processed first-come first-served. In-person application assistance is available through DHCD and the Mayor's Office of Older Adult Affairs & Advocacy. structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants apply online or submit hard copy applications at Abel Wolman Building (1st floor) or 417 E. Fayette Street (11th floor). Applicants for the 2026 Tax Sale Deferral Program are automatically reviewed for the Legacy Homeowners Pilot Program if they meet the additional criteria. The Mayor's Office of Older Adult Affairs and Advocacy conducts coordinated in-person and phone outreach through April 15 to older adults who may qualify. structured_extraction.program_name: New Construction and/or Rehabilitation of Existing Affordable Rental Housing NOFA
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Department of Housing & Community Development provides grants from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to support new construction of affordable rental housing and rehabilitation/preservation of existing rental projects for affordable housing. The program includes set-asides for Community Land Trusts and emerging developers. Multiple rounds of funding are offered with varying amounts and timelines, with up to $7,000,000 to $7,500,000 available depending on the funding round. Individual projects can request funding amounts with specific set-asides of up to $1,000,000 for Community Land Trusts and up to $1,000,000 for emerging developers. Emerging developers are defined as those who have completed at least three and no more than five projects. Projects must be completed and occupied within 2 years of Funding Agreement execution. Funds serve households earning 50% or less of Area Median Income (AMI), with at least half of units serving households at 30% or less AMI. A minimum 30-year affordability restriction is required.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants ranging from up to $1,000,000 per project to up to $7,500,000 total available from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund depending on funding round. Individual projects can request funding amounts with specific set-asides of up to $1,000,000 for Community Land Trusts and up to $1,000,000 for emerging developers. Funding supports new construction of affordable rental housing and rehabilitation/preservation of existing rental projects. Maximum funding is 50% of project's Total Development Cost or $1,000,000 per project, whichever is less. Per-unit maximums: $75,000 for 50% AMI households; $120,000 per unit for fewer than 10 units at 30% AMI; $150,000 per unit for 10 or more units at 30% AMI. Up to 25% of award combined for predevelopment and acquisition costs. Up to 10% for operating costs directly related to project implementation. Up to 25% of award can be advanced for predevelopment/acquisition costs (grants only). Funds can support construction costs including builder's profit, overhead, and construction management; architecture and engineering fees; personnel and consultant costs; and prevailing wage rates for all employees including City Prevailing Wage rates.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Opioid Restitution Fund provides community grants funded through opioid settlement recovery to support nonprofit organizations and other eligible entities leading efforts to address substance use prevention, treatment, recovery, and harm reduction, including the social determinants of health, and to redress or prevent other harms caused by the opioid epidemic. The fund was established by Mayor Brandon Scott's August 2024 Executive Order to receive Baltimore City's opioid settlement recoveries and sustain their impact for at least 15 years. A total of $2 million is available for allocation in Round 1 (Fiscal Year 2026). Proposed project funding amounts can be spread across a project period of up to two years. Organizations that choose to use their full award within a single year are still eligible to apply for funding in the following year. Funding is distributed across three tiers, with final award amounts determined based on the scope of work and available funding.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A total of $2 million is available for allocation in Round 1 (Fiscal Year 2026). Funding is distributed across three tiers: Tier 1 (up to $50,000, approximately 3-6 awards) for low-barrier social support services including housing, transportation, food assistance, education, and employment; Tier 2 (up to $250,000, approximately 2-4 awards) for comprehensive low-barrier harm reduction services including naloxone distribution, drug checking, syringe service programs, and wound care; Tier 3 (up to $500,000, approximately 2-3 awards) for low-barrier mobile treatment services in disproportionately affected geographic areas with robust harm reduction components. Proposed project funding amounts can be spread across a project period of up to two years. Organizations that choose to use their full award within a single year are still eligible to apply for funding in the following year. Grants support programs, services, and supports that address substance use prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, and social determinants of health.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Proposals due November 23, 2025, 11:59 p.m. EST; Full applications due January 25, 2026, 11:59 p.m. EST
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit organizations and other eligible entities in Baltimore City working on opioid crisis response, overdose prevention, treatment, harm reduction, recovery, and addressing the social determinants of health. Priority given to organizations with proven experience serving opioid-impacted populations in Baltimore City, including those with local yearly operating budgets under $15 million.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Allowable uses: Programs, services, and supports that address substance use prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, and social determinants of health; addressing overdose and substance use disorder; redressing or preventing other harms caused by the opioid epidemic; peer staff employment; medication-assisted treatment (MOUD); naloxone and harm reduction supplies distribution; overdose prevention education; case management and peer support services; housing, transportation, food assistance; behavioral health counseling; community events; small-scale improvements directly supporting service delivery (e.g., harm reduction spaces, mobile treatment outfitting); vehicle/van purchases if correlated to specific tier activities. Unallowable uses: Law enforcement salaries and equipment; drug courts; mandatory or abstinence-only treatment; coercive services; stigmatizing materials; large-scale or long-term capital construction projects; fundraising; overhead above 15% of grant award; duplicative services already funded through Statewide Settlements; law enforcement or carceral approaches; discriminatory practices. Allowable uses are outlined in the RFP documentation. Unallowable uses are detailed in Appendix A.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. Organizations must have operating offices in Baltimore City and demonstrate direct service experience with opioid-affected populations in Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Must be a nonprofit organization (501(c)(3) status required for Tier 2 and Tier 3 applications; not required for Tier 1)

Must operate in Baltimore City with operating office and direct service experience
Must be in good standing with State of Maryland and City of Baltimore
Must be in good financial standing with valid EIN
Must align with opioid crisis response priorities and the City's approved uses to address overdose and substance use disorder
Grants must support prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, and social determinants of health that redress or prevent other harm caused by the opioid epidemic

Must comply with all grant policies, procedures, grant terms, and conditions outlined in the grant agreement
Grantees must meet fiscal monitoring requirements and submit monthly financial documentation by the 15th of the subsequent month
Must maintain written time, attendance, and overtime policies; staff time allocation cannot exceed 100% of compensated time
Must demonstrate 5+ years of proven experience in Baltimore City serving opioid-impacted populations (as of Round 1 FY2026)
Overhead costs cannot exceed 15% of grant award
Must provide accurate, honest, and timely information in applications
Must self-assess project eligibility before submitting; seek prior approval of all relevant parties
Must complete projects per approved scope of work and timeline
Must retain final reports for future audits
Must return unused funding

Activities must correlate to specific tier within program
Activities must be implementable and measurable within two-year grant period

Detailed scope of work with clear objectives and deliverables required

Sustainability plan beyond ORF grant funding required
