structured_extraction.program_description: Project Restore 2.0 is a grant program funded through American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds that provides financial support to place-based economic development organizations (such as Main Streets, Arts and Entertainment Districts, community development corporations, and other economic development entities) and businesses to improve the vitality of Maryland's commercial corridors and incentivize commercial investment in vacant retail and commercial properties. The program offers multiple grant opportunities: the Rental Assistance Grant (up to $30,000 for one year of rent assistance at maximum $2,500 per month for small businesses with 50 or fewer employees), the Business Operations Grant (up to $250,000 per year for 1 or 2 years based on sales and use tax generated), and grants up to $300,000 for place-based economic development organizations in designated Sustainable Communities to sub-grant to businesses. Grants support activating vacant buildings, supporting small businesses, creating jobs, improving commercial corridors, and enabling businesses opening or expanding into vacant retail and commercial properties to receive assistance with rent payments, operating costs, staff costs, capital improvements, marketing, inventory and supplies, utilities, renovation, equipment, and other eligible expenses in their first year of operation. Place-based organizations receive grants to identify priority vacant storefronts and buildings in business districts, then sub-grant funding to businesses for rental assistance, renovation, equipment, and operating costs.

Grant awards distributed in prior rounds have ranged from $54,716 to $300,000. Up to 15% of the grant request can support operating costs and administrative expenses for the grantee organization, including staff costs, professional services, and software/equipment related to grant administration. Grant funds can support rent payments (at market rate), operating costs, staff costs, capital improvements, marketing, inventory and supplies, utilities, renovation, equipment, furniture, fixtures, and commercial investment in vacant retail and commercial spaces in the first year of operation, but cannot be used for acquisition/building purchase, new construction, vehicles, executive salaries or bonuses, reimbursement for previously incurred costs, or water/sewer infrastructure upgrades. No match requirement. Payments are made quarterly upon approval of Request for Payment/Progress Report before construction/purchasing begins. Organizations receiving funds sub-grant to eligible businesses for rental assistance, renovation, and equipment to activate vacant storefronts and buildings in local business districts. All funds must be expended and businesses open by December 31, 2025. Stackable with other State funds.

structured_extraction.program_description: Rental Housing Works is a gap financing program that provides subordinate loans to create jobs and strengthen the Maryland economy by supporting the creation and preservation of affordable rental housing. The financing is used alongside the Multifamily Bond Program and 4% Low Income Housing Tax Credits. Subordinate loans are funded from State general obligation bonds with a 40-year term, 2% simple interest, and payments limited to 75% of annual cash flow. Loans are due on sale, refinancing, transfer of property, or default. The maximum loan amount per project is $2.5 million, though this limit may be waived in certain circumstances such as unexpected interest rate volatility, balancing department resources, or projects with significant economic impact and job creation. Funding is limited to the amount necessary to make the project financially feasible and viable in accordance with Section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis with funding awarded based on readiness to proceed.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federal Treasury-allocated program providing loan capital to Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) matched with private capital for relending to small businesses throughout Maryland. DHCD issues SSBCI Loans to CDFIs, which are then relent to small businesses. Designed to provide flexible financing for start-ups and new/existing business expansions with a focus on CDFI investment areas and emphasis on underserved entrepreneurs, particularly those owned and operated by socially and economically disadvantaged individuals (SEDI) and very small businesses (VSB). Individual loans to small businesses are targeted up to $250,000, while CDFI loans range from $2,000,000 to $15,000,000 based on their relending capacity. With specific allocations for very small businesses (VSB) and socially and economically disadvantaged individual (SEDI) owned businesses.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: SSBCI Loans to CDFIs: 0%-2% interest, up to 7-year term with annual renewal options, maximum $5,000,000 SSBCI funding per lender, maximum total financing $20,000,000. CDFIs receive loans ranging from $2,000,000 to $15,000,000 based on their capacity for relending to small businesses. Individual small business loans from CDFIs: Up to $250,000, maximum 18% interest, up to 5-year terms (longer for asset acquisition). Combined origination fee and points capped at 1%; application fee maximum $100. Loans require private capital match with initial structure of 20% SSBCI/80% private for non-SEDI businesses, and 30% SSBCI/70% private for SEDI and VSB businesses. CDFIs must maintain 20% at risk. Funds for working capital, marketing, real estate down payments, renovations, equipment acquisition, and business expansion costs. Applications processed on a first-come, first-served basis.

structured_extraction.program_description: Section 811 is a federally funded, project-based rental assistance program administered by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development in partnership with the Maryland Department of Disabilities and the Maryland Department of Health. The program expands affordable housing for low-income adults with disabilities by providing rental assistance tied to specific units in approved rental housing projects. Section 811 helps eligible residents live in stable housing with access to supportive services and enables people with disabilities to live independently in the community. Participants pay 30% of their income toward rent and utilities, and the program pays the remaining rent directly to the landlord. Funds are awarded to eligible rental projects that receive federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits or State Rental Housing Funds. The program links affordable housing with voluntary community-based long-term support services for extremely low-income nonelderly persons with disabilities. Authorized under Section 811 of the Cranston-Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. 8013, as amended by the Frank Melville Supportive Housing Investment Act of 2010, the program features minimum 20-year rental assistance contracts with potential for renewal based on HUD requirements and appropriations. The program aims to identify, stimulate, and support innovative state-level strategies that transform and increase housing for persons with disabilities while providing access to appropriate support and services.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Section 811 provides project-based rental assistance to subsidize rent and utilities for eligible residents. Participants pay 30% of their income toward rent and utilities, and the program pays the remaining rent directly to the landlord. Funds are awarded to eligible rental projects that receive federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits or State Rental Housing Funds. Eligible properties receive assistance to support unit subsidies for people with disabilities. Monthly rental assistance payments to owners equal the difference between contract rent and tenant rent owed by eligible tenants. Initial lease terms are 1 year, with automatic renewal for successive one-month terms thereafter. Rent and utility assistance is calculated at 30% of the tenant's income, with the program paying the remaining rent directly to the landlord. The tenant is responsible for paying utilities and their 30% share of combined rent and utilities. Eligible properties receive assistance to support unit subsidies for people with disabilities. Rental Assistance Contracts (RACs) are executed between Grantees and property Owners for designated Assisted Units within properties. Gross rent may not exceed Fair Market Rent (FMR) unless substantiated by market study. Annual rent adjustments based on HUD's Operating Cost Adjustment Factor (OCAF) or other HUD-approved operating cost index. Vacancy payments may be made to owners for vacant Assisted Units (up to 80% of contract rent for up to 60 days under specified conditions). Administrative Costs up to 8% of annual Section 811 PRA award. Initial Project Rental Assistance must cover five years of funding with minimum 20-year period of performance. After the initial 5-year funding cycle, renewals are subject to annual Congressional appropriations. Grants range from minimum $2 million to maximum $12 million per award. Maryland Received $9,808,054 in Fiscal Year 2013 to provide project-based assistance for 150 units statewide, with approximately 75% of units expected in the Baltimore and Washington, D.C. areas and 25% distributed on the Eastern Shore and Western Maryland. In Fiscal Year 2012, Maryland received $11,229,308 to provide project-based assistance for 150 units in the Baltimore and Washington D.C. Metropolitan Statistical Areas. Security deposit (one month's payment or $50, whichever is greater). Pet deposits capped at $300 maximum; cannot be required for assistance animals. Funds must be disbursed by September 30, 2025. Lease automatically renews for successive one-month terms after initial 1-year term. Grantee makes Project Rental Assistance Payments covering the difference between Contract Rent and tenant-paid portion. Utility allowance provisions included when utility allowance exceeds family contribution. Financial assistance to property owners for rental housing units occupied by persons with disabilities. Rental assistance payments to owners. Additional payments when Utility Allowance exceeds Total Tenant Payment. Vacancy payments up to 80% of contract rent for up to 60 days. No late payment fees for assisted units. Utility reimbursements must be disbursed within 5 business days. structured_extraction.application_process_overview: DHCD meets with an Interagency Committee including representatives from the Maryland Department of Disabilities (MDOD) and Maryland Department of Health (MDH) to review projects that align with program goals. Once a project is selected, DHCD issues a Reservation Award Letter to the developer confirming eligibility for funding to support unit subsidies for people with disabilities. For individuals, contact your case manager, support planner, resource coordinator, coordinator of community service, or community health worker to complete the pre-screening and application process. Contact the Maryland Department of Disabilities for application details. Waiting lists for rent subsidy programs may be long, so applicants are encouraged to apply as soon as possible. For applications, submit electronically via Grants.gov unless waiver granted for paper submission. Waiver request must be submitted in advance. Upon acceptable completion of the housing project, Owner and Grantee execute Section 811 Rental Assistance Contract. Preliminary award selection is followed by negotiation phase, with technical assistance provided via webinars, conferences, and quarterly conference calls. Multi-part application includes: Abstract/Summary (3-5 pages), Partnership Agreement, Narrative Response to 5 Rating Factors (maximum 45 pages), General Application Requirements and Certifications, and Supporting Documents/Attachments. Electronic submission via Grants.gov required unless waivered for paper submission. Paper application deadline is 3:59:59 p.m. eastern time on deadline date. Waiver requests must be submitted no later than 15 days prior to application deadline. For individuals: Case manager assists with application submission via SocialServe web-based Waitlist Registry system; Pre-screening determines eligibility; Full application follows; Background check review; Waitlist Registry documentation; Transfer request process with county preferences; Applicant receives date/time stamp of application submission; Applicant accepts or declines unit offers within 5 business days; Up to 3 units offered before Exceptions Committee review if all declined. Upon acceptable project completion, Grantee and Owner execute Section 811 Rental Assistance Contract with property for rental assistance. Lease automatically renews for successive one-month terms. Move-in inspection required with both owner and eligible family present. Any deficiencies must be remedied within 30 days of tenant move-in. Compile necessary identity and income verification documents including photo identification, Social Security Award letters, Social Security Card, and paystubs. Multi-part application submission via Grants.gov with Abstract/Summary (3-5 pages), Partnership Agreement documentation, Narrative Response to 5 Rating Factors (maximum 45 pages), General Application Requirements and Certifications, Supporting Documents/Commitment Letters. HUD staff may provide general guidance before deadline but cannot assist with application preparation. Process involves multiple stakeholders: DHCD, Housing providers, Case Managers, Tenants, MDOD (Maryland Department of Disabilities), and DHMH (Department of Health and Mental Hygiene). Includes Unit Identification and Turnover Process. Includes PRA Tenant Issue Process. Submit transfer request with documentation; Receive list of available properties matching needs and preferences; Accept or decline unit offers within 5 business days; Up to 3 units offered; declining all 3 triggers Exceptions Committee review; Waitlist Manager maintains transfer request list by timestamp.

structured_extraction.program_name: Seed Community Development Anchor Institution Fund
structured_extraction.program_description: This program provides competitive grants and loans to anchor institutions (colleges, universities, and hospitals) for community development and capital improvement projects that generate jobs, strengthen partnerships between institutions and Maryland communities, and create safer, healthier, and more attractive communities. Capital funding supports projects in Sustainable Communities or areas of the state that have not been invested in, including construction of facilities serving as hubs for workforce training, skilled trades education, entrepreneurship, and community access. The program also supports community development through workforce training, economic development, healthcare access, housing, community spaces, and infrastructure improvements. Projects may include construction, renovation, design, engineering, predevelopment, and infrastructure projects. Project amounts range from $100,000 to $3,000,000 with total program allocation of $10,000,000.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants and loans for capital improvement projects. Project amounts range from $100,000 to $3,000,000 with total program allocation of $10,000,000. Applicants must provide matching funds equal to the amount of financial assistance received from the fund (1:1 match requirement). Fund supports construction, renovation, design, engineering, predevelopment, and infrastructure projects including workforce hubs, business incubators, health facilities, housing, community centers, and streetscape improvements. Equipment purchases such as medical equipment and operational support are also eligible.

structured_extraction.program_audience: Anchor institutions defined as institutions of higher education in Maryland or hospital institutions in Maryland; colleges, universities, health systems, community development corporations, municipal governments, and redevelopment authorities serving low-to-moderate income residents and communities committed to community engagement and economic development.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Capital improvement projects including construction and renovation, design and engineering services, predevelopment activities, infrastructure improvements (sewer, stormwater, HVAC, electrical), equipment purchases such as medical equipment, CT imaging, and dental services, workforce training facilities, affordable housing development, community spaces and facilities, ADA accessibility improvements, and land acquisition.

Geographic eligibility can be determined using the Neighborhood Revitalization Mapper. Available to eligible anchor institutions statewide with geographic focus on Baltimore City (primary), Anne Arundel County (Brooklyn Park, Baybrook areas), Pikesville, Baltimore County, Kent County, Dorchester County, and Somerset County.

structured_extraction.program_name: Shelter and Transitional Housing Facilities Grant Program
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides capital financing for emergency shelters and transitional housing facilities that provide housing and support services to prevent homelessness and assist households to live independently. The program uses a Harm Reduction approach for supportive services. Funding helps reduce homelessness in Maryland by supporting new construction, acquisition, rehabilitation of housing, and purchase of capital equipment for transitional housing and emergency shelters that include supportive services for residents.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Capital financing for new construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and alteration of housing, and purchase of capital equipment. Grant funds generally may not exceed 50 percent of total development costs, except under certain conditions where up to 75 percent is allowed. Eligible uses include land and building acquisition, site preparation and development, construction, rehabilitation and improvement of structures, architectural and engineering services, machinery, equipment, and furnishings, bonds, insurance, and fees related to real estate development. Roofs must meet 20-year, no-dollar-limit warranty requirement. Recipients must maintain the property as transitional housing or emergency shelter for 15 years or repay the grant. Cannot fund supportive services directly or religious purposes.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Applications accepted year-round on first-come, first-served basis
structured_extraction.contact_name: Shelter and Transitional Housing Grant Program Coordinator
structured_extraction.program_audience: 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations and local governments seeking to develop transitional housing and emergency shelter facilities for homeless or at-risk individuals and families, including families, women and children, single males, and victims of domestic violence.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Land and building acquisition, site preparation and development, new construction, acquisition, alteration, conversion, relocation, renovation, replacement, restoration, and rehabilitation of housing structures, architectural and engineering services, machinery and equipment (HVAC systems, furnishings), utilities installation and extension, bonds, insurance, and fees related to real estate development. Studies, surveys, plans, specifications, appraisals, and environmental impact reports. Site development and improvements including grading, drainage, roads, parking, landscaping, and lighting. Initial equipment and furnishings with 15-year life expectancy and durability requirements. Building code compliance work. Roofs must meet 20-year, no-dollar-limit warranty requirement. Cannot fund supportive services directly or religious purposes.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide. Projects with new construction must be located in Priority Funding Areas (PFAs), which include all incorporated municipalities with some exceptions, areas between Baltimore beltway and city limits, areas between Washington DC beltway and boundary, Sustainable Communities, federal and state enterprise zones, county-designated PFAs and rural villages, and certified heritage areas within locally designated growth areas. Local government letters of support are required for all projects.

Contact the Housing Development Programs office for application submission procedures.

structured_extraction.program_name: Special Loans Program – Indoor Plumbing Program
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides low-interest or deferred loans to owner-occupants and rental property owners to install, repair, or replace indoor plumbing systems in residential properties. Assistance covers wells, septic systems, piping, connections to public water or sewer systems, plumbing fixtures, bathrooms and toilets, water purification systems, sand mound systems, and replacement of lead pipes inside homes after service line replacement. The program serves individuals and non-profits with limited income to finance additions or repairs to water or sewer systems in structurally sound properties. Interest rates range from 0% to 6% based on the applicant's ability to pay. Maximum loan term is 30 years. Deferred loans are available to borrowers requiring health, safety or accessibility improvements, with potential annual forgiveness for families with incomes below 30 percent of statewide or Washington, D.C. Metropolitan Statistical Area median income. Also provides financial assistance to homeowners who need to replace lead pipes inside their homes after the city replaces the lead service line up to the home's entrance.

list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing

For 80% AMI: 4.5% - 6.0% interest rates; For 60% AMI: 0% - 4.5% interest rates. Maximum loan amount is $50,000. Maximum loan term is 20 to 30 years depending on county. Loans over $5,000 or with deferred payments are secured by mortgage. Deferred loans are available to borrowers requiring health, safety or accessibility improvements. Deferred loan amounts or portions may be forgiven annually for families with incomes below 30 to 50 percent of statewide or Washington, D.C. Metropolitan Statistical Area median income.

structured_extraction.program_description: A loan program designed to preserve and improve single-family owner-occupied homes by bringing properties up to applicable building codes and standards or minimum housing quality standards. This income-targeted financing program provides zero percent interest loans that are fully deferred and secured by a mortgage, with maximum loan amounts generally at 100 percent of property value. Low-interest loans (0-6%) are also available for critical home repairs with maximum loan amount of $50,000 and maximum term of 30 years. Eligible repairs include mold remediation, gas leaks, roof repair/replacement, asbestos abatement, lead abatement, plumbing/electrical/HVAC repairs, foundation waterproofing, radon mitigation, windows/doors (health and safety only), structural repairs, accessibility modifications, pest treatments, ductwork upgrades, and other critical health and safety repairs.

structured_extraction.program_description: A comprehensive suite of funding programs to support revitalization goals of communities across Maryland. The State Revitalization Programs consist of seven primary programs: Baltimore Regional Neighborhood Initiative, Community Legacy, Maryland Façade Improvement Program, National Capital Strategic Economic Development Fund, Seed Community Development Anchor Institution Fund, Strategic Demolition Fund – Statewide, and Baltimore Vacants Reinvestment Initiative (Project C.O.R.E.). These programs work with local partners to bring new investment and vitality to Maryland's core communities through a broad range of loan, grant, and technical assistance programs. Projects should connect to community revitalization strategies and goals from a Sustainable Community Action Plan and result in lasting infrastructure with at least a 15-year lifespan. The program supports neighborhood projects including upper story redevelopment, commercial facade improvements, adaptive reuse of vacant properties, neighborhood parks, arts and cultural amenities, small business incubators, and shared community spaces. State funding is applied for annually to support neighborhood projects and shared spaces in eligible Maryland Sustainable Communities.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants, loans, and technical assistance for capital projects located within Sustainable Communities and eligible areas. Funding supports neighborhood projects including upper story residential redevelopment, commercial facade improvements, adaptive reuse of vacant properties, neighborhood parks, arts and cultural amenities, small business incubators, residential property acquisition and rehabilitation, and community open spaces. FY2026 budgeted funding includes: Baltimore Regional Neighborhood Initiative ($18MM capital, $499,486 operating); Community Legacy ($8MM capital); Maryland Façade Improvement Program ($5MM capital); National Capital Strategic Economic Development Fund ($18MM capital, $200,000 operating). Capital projects must have at least a 15-year shelf life. Operating expenses (staff salaries, feasibility studies, marketing, maintenance) are permitted for BRNI and NED programs only. State funding is applied for annually to support neighborhood projects and shared spaces.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Capital projects with at least a 15-year shelf life, including demolition of derelict structures, site acquisition and assembly, site development/infrastructure improvements, architectural and engineering designs, building stabilization and structural repairs, environmental remediation, upper story residential redevelopment, commercial facade improvements, adaptive reuse of vacant properties, neighborhood parks, arts and cultural amenities, small business incubators, community open space, neighborhood beautification, acquisition or rehabilitation of vacant residential properties, new construction, park/playground construction, real property acquisition and down payment assistance, historic property stabilization, and housing production (mixed-income, middle market, affordable). Operating expenses for BRNI and NED programs only (staffing, project administration, feasibility/marketing studies, maintenance). Indirect costs up to 15%.

All projects must be located within designated Sustainable Communities and help achieve outcomes identified in the community's Sustainable Communities Action Plan. Baltimore Regional Neighborhood Initiative: Baltimore City, inner-beltway communities of Baltimore County and Anne Arundel County. National Capital Strategic Economic Development Fund: Prince George's County and Montgomery County (specific boundaries defined). Community Legacy: Statewide in Sustainable Communities; Opportunity Zones in Allegany, Garrett, Somerset and Wicomico Counties. Strategic Demolition Fund: Statewide Sustainable Communities and Opportunity Zones in Allegany, Garrett, Somerset and Wicomico Counties. Nearly 130 designated Sustainable Communities Areas across the state with at least one in each county. Eligible Maryland Sustainable Communities in Harford County.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Strategic Demolition Fund seeks to accelerate economic development and job creation in Maryland communities by improving the economic viability of greyfield development (the redevelopment of previously developed but underutilized sites). The program funds demolition of derelict structures, site acquisition and assembly to create redevelopment-sized parcels, site development, construction-level architectural and engineering designs, infrastructure improvements, historic building rehabilitation and adaptive reuse, residential and commercial property renovations, and community space development. Grants and loans support the demolition of vacant, blighted, and derelict structures as part of statewide revitalization efforts. Funds are limited and awards focus on projects with high economic and revitalization impact in their communities. Approximately $10 million in capital funding is available in Fiscal Year 2025 for strategic demolition projects in Sustainable Communities or Opportunity Zones.

Funding supports affordable housing development, recreation facilities, commercial kitchen facilities, and other community amenities. Approximately $10 million is available in Fiscal Year 2025. structured_extraction.program_description: The Sustainable Communities Program provides a geographic designation for local areas to support community development, revitalization, and sustainability through coordinated strategies. It encourages cross-governmental collaboration by providing designated Sustainable Communities with access to an interagency revitalization toolbox of financing programs and tax credit incentives. The program gives local governments and community partners resources to improve older communities and promote growth that is environmentally, economically, and socially responsible by combining resources for historic preservation, housing, and economic development under a single designation, focusing on infrastructure improvements, multimodal transportation, and development that strengthens existing communities.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides a Sustainable Community designation that qualifies local governments to apply for certain state programs including Community Legacy, Neighborhood BusinessWorks, Strategic Demolition Fund, Main Street Maryland, Maryland Façade Improvement Program, Job Creation Tax Credit, Enhanced Local Tax Increment Financing Authority, Low Income Housing Tax Credit, Water Quality Financing Administration Programs, Transportation Alternatives Program, Safe Routes to School, Sidewalk Retrofit Program, Kim Lamphier Bikeways Network Program, and other financing mechanisms. The designation is valid for five years and requires approval from an interagency panel led by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development and final approval from the Governor's Smart Growth Subcabinet. Designated communities gain access to an interagency revitalization toolbox including capital funding for business retention and attraction, homeownership, commercial revitalization, mixed-use development, streetscape improvements, sidewalk construction and replacement, bicycle access and bikeways, gap financing, subordinate financing, demolition grants, operating assistance grants, job creation tax credits, enhanced local tax increment financing, low-income housing tax credits, water quality and stormwater management financing, environmental remediation, parking facility construction, grey field development improvement, land assembly for housing and revitalization, below-market interest rate loans, loan forgiveness, reimbursable federal aid funding, facade improvements, and SHA transportation programs.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Technical Assistance Grant program assists local governments and nonprofit organizations with operating costs and professional services associated with local housing and community revitalization efforts. structured_extraction.program_name: UPLIFT (Utilizing Progressive Lending Investments to Finance Transformation)
structured_extraction.program_description: A public-private partnership housing development program that increases property values and provides wealth-building homeownership opportunities for targeted households by accelerating development, construction, and sale of quality affordable housing in low-income census tracts and designated Sustainable Communities. The program addresses the appraisal gap—the difference between the cost to develop a property and the price it can sell for on the market—which is common in neighborhoods affected by redlining and disinvestment. UPLIFT couples development loans to build new housing with a commitment from the state to offer grants and loans to nearby 'Legacy Homeowners' often living in energy inefficient and deteriorated housing. The State covers the difference between the cost to build and the sale price through UPLIFT funding to help close the gap in historically redlined and disinvested communities. The program provides support for applicant packages, underwriting, closing, and project management through an electronic submission system. The program prioritizes projects that transform the largest proportion of vacant properties in a project area and aims to reach a broad range of households across the income spectrum, especially current residents.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A public-private partnership investment program providing gap financing to cover the difference between the total eligible cost to develop a property and the price the property can sell for on the market. Selected qualified development teams acquire, develop, build, and sell quality affordable housing using a combination of public and private financing, with UPLIFT funding covering the appraisal gap. Development loans are provided for construction financing up to $75,000 per unit at 0% interest for a term equal to construction period plus three months, with a minimum of 8 units required. Homebuyers receive state promissory notes (second lien secured loans) covering the appraisal gap as part of the financing package. Homeowner Promissory Notes are offered at 0% interest rate with automatic 20% annual principal decline, fully forgiven after 5 years, with payment due only upon sale or fraud, up to $75,000 per unit. Developer loans are structured in second lien position. Minimum 25% of units must be sold to households earning 80% of Area Median Income (AMI) or below. Electronic submission system manages applicant packages, final underwriting, closing documents, draws/requisitions, and close-out submissions. A $1,000 non-refundable application fee per project is required. Origination fee of 1% of loan amount. Developer fees are paid 25% at initial closing with remainder disbursed pro rata as units sell, subject to 10% retainage.

structured_extraction.program_description: The largest residential energy conservation program in the country, WAP is a federally-funded program administered by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development that provides weatherization services to income-eligible homeowners, renters, and low-income households through a statewide network of Local Weatherization Agencies including Community Action Agencies, nonprofits, and local government agencies. The program reduces heating and cooling costs through energy-conservation measures and addresses health and safety issues in homes. Services include blower door air infiltration reduction, insulation in attic/floors/walls and crawl spaces, hot water system improvements and water heater wrapping, lighting retrofit, furnace clean/tune and safety repairs, burner retrofit or replacement, caulking and air sealing around windows and doors, HVAC and ductwork upgrades, moisture control, and health and safety items. The program enables households to lower energy bills by an average of 30 to 35 percent through comprehensive whole-house analysis using sophisticated energy modeling and diagnostic testing. Priority is given to elderly persons (age 60+), persons with disabilities, families with children under 5 years old, and households with high energy usage or energy burden. Services are delivered through home energy audits to identify needed improvements, quality control inspections, emergency heating and cooling system repairs and replacements, water heater repairs and replacements, follow-up maintenance services, on-site solar system readiness evaluations, occupant education on energy management, and weatherization readiness funds for addressing deferral conditions up to $15,000 per unit. The program provides a Standard Work Specification-aligned field guide for retrofitting homes in Maryland with technical guidance for weatherization work in single-family homes and manufactured homes, covering attic air sealing and insulation, basement/rim joist work, duct sealing/insulation, window/door work, water heater insulation, low-flow fixtures, ventilation, and manufactured home improvements aligned with National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) Standard Work Specifications (SWS). The program includes multiple funding streams: DOE WAP (federal), EmPOWER Maryland (state utility-funded), MEAP-C (critical heating/cooling/water heater repairs and replacements), and MEAP-Wx (weatherization). Comprehensive retrofit programs include Whole Home Efficiency jobs and Base Efficiency jobs with different eligibility criteria. Energy audits use Hancock/HEAT software aligned with NREL Standard Work Specifications with 60+ job aids covering air sealing, insulation, ventilation, duct sealing, and energy efficiency procedures. Program provides health and safety assessments and measures to address conditions necessary to perform effective weatherization work, governed by 10 CFR 440.16(h), 440.18(d)(15), 440.21(5), and DOE Health and Safety Guidance (WPN 22-7). Technical field guide created by Energy Smart Academy at Santa Fe Community College for the Weatherization Collaborative provides standard work specifications and field guides for weatherization work in single-family homes and manufactured homes. Health and safety component provides guidance on allowable activities and protocols for addressing hazards in homes including remediation of combustion gases and carbon monoxide, electrical hazards (including knob and tube wiring), lead-based paint, mold and moisture, fuel leaks, gas appliances, pests, radon, formaldehyde and VOCs, and hazardous materials disposal. Program addresses energy efficiency work while maintaining worker and occupant safety under DOE regulations (10 CFR 440) and WPN 22-7 guidance.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides free energy improvement services and weatherization improvements to income-eligible households. Services are determined through a comprehensive home energy audit inspection using DOE-approved tools (HEAT software). The program delivers installation of energy conservation materials including air infiltration reduction, insulation, hot water system improvements, water heater wrapping, lighting retrofit, furnace repairs and replacement, caulking and air sealing, HVAC and ductwork upgrades, moisture control, and health and safety items at no cost to eligible households. Quality control inspections and occupant education on energy management are included. Emergency heating and cooling system repairs and replacements, water heater repairs and replacements, and weatherization readiness funds for deferral condition remediation (roof, electrical, plumbing, structural repairs, mold and moisture remediation, pest removal) up to $15,000 per unit are available. Weatherization materials and labor include insulation (batts and loose fill for attics, sidewalls, basement walls, crawlspace walls), caulk, sealants, metal sheeting, duct work, duct sealing and insulation, plenums and pipes insulation, window and door installation/replacement, window glass replacement, water heater insulation (electric and gas), low-flow showerheads and faucet aerators, roof vents and exhaust ventilation, safety equipment (smoke alarms, CO detectors), lighting system upgrades (LED replacements, fixtures, controls), appliance replacement (refrigerators, Energy Star certified), and weatherstripping and door seals. Average weatherization cost per unit is approximately $7,496.27 with estimated energy savings of 29.3 MBtus per unit and average energy bill reduction of 30-35 percent. Health and Safety expenditure limit is 20 percent of per-unit cost, capped at $1,000 per job. Community Action Agencies, nonprofits, and local governments apply through Requests for Applications conducted at least every 3 years or more frequently to ensure statewide service coverage. Contractors bid to provide weatherization services through individual subgrantees. Minimum 80 percent of Program Income funds must be used for labor, materials, and program support; up to 10 percent may be used for Training and Technical Assistance. Base Efficiency jobs and Whole Home Efficiency jobs available with different eligibility criteria. Incidental repairs must have Savings to Investment Ratio (SIR) of at least 1.0 for most measures, 1.1 for others. Lead-safe work protocols required for pre-1978 homes with fit-tested respirators and specific PPE requirements including Tyvek suits, gloves, and fit-tested respirators; bearded workers must use PAPR (Powered Air-Purifying Respirator); respirators must be fit-tested annually. Compliance with NFPA codes, UL standards, ASHRAE 62.2-2016 guidelines, EPA Lead RRP Rule, and OSHA regulations required. Manual J load calculations required for heating or cooling appliance installation/replacement. Licensed HVAC installers with required licensing/certification must perform HVAC work. Energy audit must be scheduled and completed before work begins using Hancock/HEAT software, aligned with National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) Standard Work Specifications (SWS) with 60+ job aids covering air sealing, insulation, ventilation, duct sealing, and energy efficiency procedures. Health and safety funds address conditions necessary to perform effective weatherization work and are allowable for direct weatherization activities by subgrantees where costs are reasonable. Health and safety is a separate budgeting category not included in Savings to Investment Ratio calculations. Testing and remediation of combustion gases, electrical hazards, and fuel leaks are covered, along with lead-safe work practices in pre-1978 homes, mold and moisture assessment and minor repairs, pest removal where cost-effective and prevents work, radon precautionary measures, gas appliance testing and maintenance, and hazardous materials disposal. Technical guidance for weatherization work is provided through field guides aligned with Standard Work Specifications (SWS 3.0 and 4.0), covering attic preparation, air sealing techniques (top plates, soffits, chases, balloon framing, penetrations), attic insulation installation methods, basement/rim joist/crawlspace insulation, duct sealing and insulation, window and door improvements, water heater and pipe insulation, exhaust ventilation installation, subfloor air sealing and insulation, dryer venting, and low-flow fixtures installation. Health and safety protocols include: installation of radon precautionary measures based on EPA protocols; installation/replacement of smoke and CO alarms (non-operable only); fire extinguishers (when solid fuels present); ventilation systems per ASHRAE 62.2-2016; air sealing and insulation work; and client education on radon, indoor air quality, and device operation. Allowable energy efficiency-related health and safety actions must be cost-reasonable per DOE standards and taken to effectively perform weatherization work or necessary as result of weatherization work. Hazards requiring remediation include combustion gases and carbon monoxide, electrical hazards (including knob and tube wiring), lead-based paint, mold and moisture, fuel leaks, gas appliances, pests, radon, formaldehyde and VOCs, and hazardous materials disposal.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: For homeowners and renters: Contact your Local Weatherization Agency (LWA) or call the Maryland Office of Energy Efficiency at 844-400-3423 or 1-800-756-0119 to submit an application. For Baltimore County, contact the Department of Aging at aginginfo@baltimorecountymd.gov or 410-887-2594. Households may also submit an application to the Department of Housing & Community Development or submit an application for Energy Assistance through the Department of Human Services and may be screened for this program. Complete the one-stop-shop energy programs application and households will be screened for all three programs (Weatherization Assistance Program, Limited Income Energy Efficiency EmPOWER Program, and Maryland Energy Assistance Program). DHCD qualifies applicants for applicable funding sources. Applicants to Office of Home Energy Programs are automatically referred to WAP unless they opt out on the application. If eligible, receive letter with assigned contractor. Contractor contacts within 30 days to schedule in-home energy assessment. Energy audit is conducted; data collected on existing equipment; metering performed for appliances; information entered into Hancock system; replacement determinations made. After assessment, contractor completes recommended work at no cost. For contractors: Contact the Local Weatherization Agency serving your county to bid on weatherization work. For organizations interested in becoming Local Weatherization Agencies: Apply through a Request for Applications (RFA) when posted, conducted at least every 3 years or more frequently. Applicants must meet minimum qualifications and register in SAM. Subgrantee applicants must submit applications in response to the RFA by the stated deadline, including organizational documentation, Key Personnel qualifications, county service areas, and all identified contractors. May require oral presentations. State evaluates applications using specified criteria; awards granted to most advantageous applicants per county. For weatherization professionals implementing work, energy audit and data collection is conducted, installation is performed per technical specifications, and Hancock system data entry is completed for appliance replacement. Hancock/HEAT software training required for subgrantees and contractors. Administrative, financial, and client services training provided. Contact Network Partners assigned to your county for direct participation. T&TA pre-approval requests must be submitted at least one week prior to training start. EmP reimbursement requests due within two weeks of completing training. DOE quarterly reimbursement statements due on the 30th day following each quarter end. Network Partners deliver lead distribution to client homes. Lead distribution considers Network Partner proximity to client's home. Homeowners and renters contact their local weatherization agency to submit an application. Once eligibility is determined, the agency will schedule an energy audit inspection to identify needed energy improvements. Services are then provided based on the inspection results. Community Action Agencies, nonprofits, and local governments apply through periodic Request for Applications to become subgrantees. Contractors contact their local weatherization subgrantee directly to bid on weatherization services or register on vendor lists and receive mass email notifications about open procurements.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP) is the largest residential energy conservation program in the country, a federally-funded program administered by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development that provides weatherization services to income-eligible homeowners, renters, and low-income households through a statewide network of Local Weatherization Agencies including Community Action Agencies, nonprofits, and local government agencies. The program reduces heating and cooling costs through energy-conservation measures and addresses health and safety issues in homes. Services include blower door air infiltration reduction, insulation in attic/floors/walls and crawl spaces, hot water system improvements and water heater wrapping, lighting retrofit, furnace clean/tune and safety repairs, burner retrofit or replacement, caulking and air sealing around windows and doors, HVAC and ductwork upgrades, moisture control, rooftop solar installation, and health and safety items. The program enables households to lower energy bills by an average of 30 to 35 percent through comprehensive whole-house analysis using sophisticated energy modeling and diagnostic testing. Priority is given to elderly persons (age 60+), persons with disabilities, families with children under 5 years old, and households with high energy usage or energy burden. Services are delivered through home energy audits to identify needed improvements, quality control inspections, emergency heating and cooling system repairs and replacements, water heater repairs and replacements, follow-up maintenance services, on-site solar system readiness evaluations, occupant education on energy management, and weatherization readiness funds for addressing deferral conditions up to $15,000 per unit. The program includes multiple funding streams: DOE WAP (federal), EmPOWER Maryland (state utility-funded), MEAP-C (critical heating/cooling/water heater repairs and replacements), and MEAP-Wx (weatherization). Comprehensive retrofit programs include Whole Home Efficiency jobs and Base Efficiency jobs with different eligibility criteria. Energy audits use Hancock/HEAT software aligned with NREL Standard Work Specifications. The program provides health and safety assessments and measures to address conditions necessary to perform effective weatherization work. Average weatherization cost per unit is approximately $7,496.27 with estimated energy savings of 29.3 MBtus per unit.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides free energy improvement services to income-eligible households through Local Weatherization Agencies, Baltimore Ounty, Baltimore City, and Howard Ounty. Services include blower door air infiltration reduction, insulation in the attic, floors, walls, basements, and crawl spaces, hot water system improvements and water heater wrapping, lighting retrofit, furnace clean/tune, safety repairs, burner retrofit or replacement, caulking and air sealing around windows and doors, moisture control, HVAC and ductwork upgrades, rooftop solar installation, and health and safety items. Services are determined through a home energy audit inspection using DOE-approved tools (HEAT software). The program delivers installation of energy conservation materials at no cost to eligible households. Quality control inspections and occupant education on energy management are included. Emergency heating and cooling system repairs and replacements, water heater repairs and replacements, and weatherization readiness funds for deferral condition remediation (roof, electrical, plumbing, structural repairs, mold and moisture remediation, pest removal) up to $15,000 per unit are available. Weatherization materials and labor include insulation (batts and loose fill for attics, sidewalls, basement walls, crawlspace walls), caulk, sealants, metal sheeting, duct work, duct sealing and insulation, plenums and pipes insulation, window and door installation/replacement, window glass replacement, water heater insulation (electric and gas), low-flow showerheads and faucet aerators, roof vents and exhaust ventilation, safety equipment (smoke alarms, CO detectors), lighting system upgrades (LED replacements, fixtures, controls), appliance replacement (refrigerators, Energy Star certified), and weatherstripping and door seals. Mandatory measures include health and safety assessments, LED lighting, air sealing, duct sealing and insulation, and attic/wall/floor insulation. Optional measures include smart thermostats, water conservation measures, refrigerator replacement, HVAC replacements, and window replacements. Average weatherization cost per unit is approximately $7,496.27 with estimated energy savings of 29.3 MBtus per unit and average energy bill reduction of 30-35 percent. Health and Safety expenditure limit is 20 percent of per-unit cost, capped at $1,000 per job. Community Action Agencies, nonprofits, and local governments apply through Requests for Applications conducted at least every 3 years or more frequently to ensure statewide service coverage. Energy efficiency improvements and weatherization measures are provided up to $250 per home for general heat waste measures (DOE WAP funds). Furnace/AC system repair or replacement with medical documentation for at-risk occupants, asbestos identification, testing, and encapsulation, mold/biological condition remediation, and minor structural repairs are provided.

Service areas determined by Local Weatherization Agencies. Calvert, Charles, Frederick, Montgomery, Prince George's, St. Mary's specifically served with Washington Gas verification capability. State and local codes vary by jurisdiction; subgrantees responsible for knowing requirements in their service areas.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: For homeowners and renters: Contact your local weatherization agency or call 1-855-583-8976 to submit an application and learn about minimum income requirements. Households may also submit an application through the Department of Human Services and may be screened for this program. In Baltimore City, applicants can also click here to visit the online Application Portal at portal.neighborlysoftware.com/BALTIMOREMD/participant, or download the pre-application form and mail it to LIGHT Intake & Assessment Unit, 417 East Fayette Street, Suite 1125, Baltimore, MD 21202. In Baltimore County, contact the Department of Aging for application and project evaluation. In Howard County, contact the Community Action Council for more information. Once eligibility is determined, the agency will schedule an energy audit inspection to identify needed energy improvements. An energy auditor will conduct an evaluation of the home to determine areas of heat loss and air infiltration. Services are then provided based on the inspection results at no cost to the homeowner. For Community Action Agencies, nonprofits, and local governments: Apply through periodic Request for Applications to become Local Weatherization Agencies. Contractors contact their local weatherization subgrantee directly to bid on weatherization services and can register on vendor lists or receive mass email notifications about open procurements. Households are screened through the one-stop-shop energy programs application. Applicants to OHEP programs are automatically referred to WAP unless they opt out. WAP office contacts qualified applicants to arrange weatherization services. Contact the Department of Housing and Community Development Division of Homeownership and Housing Preservation for more information and to apply. Distribution through subgrantee network via email and conference calls. Q&A recorded and posted on subgrantee website. Monitoring visits conducted by DHCD. Tracking forms maintained for all monitoring visits.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland State Small Business Credit Initiative (SSBCI) Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A federal program administered by the state that expands access to capital for small businesses throughout Maryland. The program provides funding for small business financing programs including flexible direct loans, capital access programs, loan participations, loan guarantees, collateral support, and equity investments to catalyze small business sustainability and expansion. It targets small businesses, micro-businesses, socially and economically disadvantaged businesses (SEDI), and technology and life sciences companies with limited opportunities for growth. The program allocates up to $50 million through the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO) to support small technology and life sciences businesses across Maryland through venture capital, startup funding, and investment programs focused on disadvantaged entrepreneurs. The Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) offers flexible financing mechanisms designed to maximize community benefit, focusing on communities with high concentrations of small, micro, and disadvantaged businesses with borrowers typically having 500 or fewer employees.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: SSBCI provides funding through loans, equity investments, and other financial assistance mechanisms. Direct loans are issued by DHCD with flexible terms designed to maximize community benefit. Loan amounts range from $500,000 minimum to $5 million maximum with terms up to 30 years in senior or subordinate loan positions. Total project costs cannot exceed $20 million. A minimum 1:1 private capital match is required with the private capital lender licensed and active in Maryland small business lending. Interest rates are determined through underwriting analysis. Fees include $250 application fee, $250 closing fee, and 1% origination fee. The program also offers capital access programs to help businesses access credit, loan participations where the program shares loan risk with lenders, loan guarantees that reduce lender risk, collateral support to help businesses secure loans, and venture equity programs for business investment. Up to $50 million is allocated through four programs administered by TEDCO: Venture Equity Fund, Venture Capital Limited Partnership Equity program, Seed Funds Equity program, and Social Impact Funds. Eligible uses include machinery and equipment purchase, working capital, owner-occupied real estate acquisition or renovation (minimum 51% owner-occupied for renovation; 60% for new construction), passive real estate acquisition or maintenance, debt refinancing (not with same lender), and stock purchases (limited to majority ESOP or worker cooperatives). Payment of back taxes with payment plan is eligible. Funds are administered through lending partners including Lendistry, City First Enterprises, FSC First, and the Community Development Fund. Technical assistance is also available through the MD Business Opportunity Center and F3Tech's SEDI Program to help with loan packaging and financial advisory services. The program does not provide grant funds.

structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland-based small businesses with 500 or fewer employees, micro-businesses, technology businesses, life sciences businesses, and Socially and Economically Disadvantaged Individuals (SEDI) seeking capital for growth, maintenance, or expansion. Businesses with significant community impact prioritized including those supporting job retention/creation, childcare, fresh food access, and community revitalization.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Machinery and equipment purchase, working capital, owner-occupied real estate acquisition or renovation (minimum 51% owner-occupied for renovation; 60% for new construction), passive real estate acquisition or maintenance, debt refinancing (not with same lender), and stock purchases (limited to majority ESOP or worker cooperatives). Payment of back taxes with payment plan is eligible. Tenant improvement spaces. Funds support projects sustaining or expanding small business operations. Business financing and growth support in communities with high concentrations of small, micro, and SEDI businesses through capital access programs, loan participations, loan guarantees, collateral support, venture equity investments, and equity investment for technology-based and life sciences businesses and startups. Ineligible uses: federal or state income tax arrears, trust/escrow account taxes, current stockholder equity acquisition, political lobbying, improvement of federally-guaranteed loans, conflicts of interest, and passive real estate investments without community benefit.

structured_extraction.program_description: A loan program designed to preserve and improve single-family owner-occupied homes and small rental properties by bringing properties up to applicable building codes and standards or minimum housing quality standards. STAR loans may also be used to build replacement houses under certain conditions, or for rehabilitation to correct deficiencies, energy conservation, handicapped accessibility, plumbing, wells, sewer, and lead hazard reduction for properties serving special housing needs. The program provides zero percent interest loans that are fully deferred and secured by a mortgage, with maximum loan amounts generally at 100 percent of property value or 110 percent of the after-rehab value. Low-interest loans (0-6%) are also available for critical home repairs with maximum loan amount of $50,000 and maximum term of 30 years. Eligible repairs include mold remediation, gas leaks, roof repair/replacement, asbestos abatement, lead abatement, plumbing/electrical/HVAC repairs, foundation waterproofing, radon mitigation, windows/doors (health and safety only), structural repairs, accessibility modifications, pest treatments, ductwork upgrades, and other critical health and safety repairs. Loans are funded with federal HOME funds. Frederick County offers loans with interest rates based on household income. Deferred payment options are available for households with income below 50 percent of the Washington D.C. MSA median income.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Zero percent interest loans that are fully deferred and secured by a mortgage or Deed of Trust, or loans with interest rates based on household income. Maximum loan is generally 100 percent of the property value or 110 percent of the after-rehab value, with exceptions considered on a case-by-case basis. Low-interest loans (0-6%) available for critical home repairs with maximum loan amount of $50,000 and maximum term of 30 years. Loans in excess of $5,000 or with deferred payments are secured by a mortgage. Household income of owner-occupants generally cannot exceed 50 percent of the area median income as published by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, though some loans may be made to households with incomes at or below 30 percent of the Washington D.C. Metropolitan Statistical Area median income, up to 55 percent of statewide median income with poor credit rating, or in exceptional cases up to 80 percent of HUD-defined median income. Grants may be considered on a case-by-case basis. Property must meet HUD's definition of modest housing. Deferred payment of principal and interest available for households with income below 50 percent of the Washington D.C. MSA median income. Loan proceeds may be used for rehabilitation, energy conservation, handicapped accessibility, plumbing, wells, sewer, lead hazard reduction, and critical health and safety repairs.

structured_extraction.program_description: A program that helps low-income households pay off large past-due electric and gas bills. Eligible customers can receive grants toward their past-due balances to help them avoid utility service termination and reduce their accumulated debt. Customers must have a past-due bill of $300 or greater to be eligible. Eligible customers may receive a grant of up to $2,000 toward their past-due electric bill or up to $1,000 toward their past-due gas bill. Households with vulnerable members (age 60 or older, under age 2, or medically fragile) may be eligible to receive the benefit again if the previously received benefit was less than $2,000 and the current past-due balance exceeds $300. Customers may receive an arrearage grant once every five years, with an exception for grants received between January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2021, which do not count towards the five-year limitation. Funding for arrearages is limited. Part of Maryland's Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants up to $2,000 towards past-due electric bills (Electric ARA) and up to $1,000 towards past-due natural gas bills (Gas ARA). Minimum arrearage balance is $300. Households with vulnerable members (age 60 or older, under age 2, or medically fragile) may be eligible to receive the benefit again if the previously received benefit was less than $2,000 and the current past-due balance exceeds $300. Customers may receive an arrearage grant once every five years, with an exception for grants received between January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2021, which do not count towards the five-year limitation. Grant is sent to the electric or gas company. Funding for arrearages is limited. Non-repayable financial assistance.

structured_extraction.program_description: Provides financial assistance and aide services to adults with disabilities to help with personal care (such as dressing, bathing, grooming, and transferring), chore services (such as cooking, laundry, light cleaning, and shopping), transportation, and activities of daily living. The program helps adults aged 18 and older with severe chronic or severe physical disabilities, or functional disabilities, remain living at home and avoid moving to nursing homes or other institutional placements. Services are provided on a sliding-scale fee basis depending on income and family size. Ongoing case management is also provided to help with planning and exploring other needed services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides financial assistance on a sliding-scale fee basis to pay for aide services in the person's home for personal care, household chores, transportation, and activities of daily living. Depending on the applicant's income and family size, the applicant may need to contribute toward the hourly cost of the aide service. The fee is paid to the Department of Social Services. The availability of funding for the program determines the number of individuals who can be served statewide. Ongoing case management is provided to help with planning and exploring other needed services.

structured_extraction.program_name: Center for Excellence in Resource Family Development (CfE)
structured_extraction.program_description: A four-year federal grant program ($8 million from the Children's Bureau) that develops and implements a model to recruit, prepare, and support resource families (foster and kinship parents) to provide enhanced services to children in out-of-home care and support their birth families toward reunification. The program prepares and supports resource parents and families of origin to partner in shared parenting using evidence-based parenting approaches. It aims to improve engagement and retention of resource families, reduce congregate care placements, and achieve improved permanency outcomes for children through five core strategies: setting expectations for co-parenting, preparing resource families and child welfare workers, recruiting and supporting resource parents, and delivering comprehensive support services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: $8 million federal cooperative agreement from the Children's Bureau spread over four years (beginning October 1, 2019 through September 30, 2023). Resource parents receive board rates and differential CfE rates for eligible children placed in CfE resource homes, plus treatment foster care difficulty of care stipends, holding rates for homes without immediate placements, and bed retainer rates to reserve space for CfE-eligible youth. Participating resource parents receive additional training including KEEP or KEEP SAFE (16-week evidence-based programs with 90-minute weekly sessions), prerequisite training on birth parent partnership, weekly support and training group sessions, mobile response and stabilization services (MRSS) for mental health crises, planned and emergency respite care, increased case management support, peer support through cohorts, and compensation ($25 gift card per completed training module) for time spent in training and additional support provided to youth and birth families. Birth families participate in Parenting Through Change for Reunification (PTC-R) group training (10 weeks of group sessions plus 6 weeks of transition support). Workforce training includes 'Promoting Parent Partnership' modules for child welfare workers and supervisors. Childcare and refreshments provided during sessions.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Resource families (foster parents and kinship parents) caring for children ages 4-18 in out-of-home care, families of origin (birth parents with reunification or guardianship goals), child welfare workers from local departments of social services, and LDSS supervisors and administrators. Participation is by selection through local departments of social services.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training and support services for resource parents in caring for children with challenging behaviors, building relationships with birth families, and supporting reunification. Services include evidence-based parenting programs (KEEP, KEEP SAFE, PTC-R, PTC-RH), peer support, case management, mental health crisis response through mobile response and stabilization services, respite care, and professional development for child welfare workforce on parent partnership practices. Funds also support staff training and certification in evidence-based models, development of training materials and curricula, implementation oversight and coaching, capacity building for model delivery, and technical assistance and evaluation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Five pilot Maryland counties: Baltimore County, Carroll County, Frederick County, Montgomery County, and Prince George's County. Selected local departments of social services are participating sites. The program prioritizes areas of the state with the highest numbers of child removals. Geographic data is used to strengthen local recruitment so children removed from their homes are more likely to remain in their communities of origin.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Local departments of social services select resource parents to participate. Local sites applied to the CfE through a standardized application assessing readiness and capacity, which was rated on a rubric with follow-up phone interviews. Once selected for participation, resource parents engage in prerequisite training on birth parent partnership, KEEP or KEEP SAFE programs, and ongoing support services through the Quality Improvement Collaborative. LDSS form local Implementation Teams with multidisciplinary representation. Participants complete training modules and post-training feedback surveys. Fidelity monitoring and coaching provided throughout implementation.

structured_extraction.program_description: CAPE is a job-driven employment program that provides free job training and support services to non-custodial parents owing child support in Washington County. The program helps participants obtain and maintain unsubsidized, competitive employment to establish a pattern of regular child support payments and overcome employment barriers. Training is available in industries including welding, green construction, machining, healthcare, and hospitality. Participants who successfully complete the program may earn forgiveness for child support arrears owed to the State of Maryland.

Participants who successfully complete the program may earn forgiveness for child support arrears owed to the State of Maryland.

structured_extraction.program_description: A statewide financial assistance program administered by the Maryland Department of Human Services Office of Home Energy Programs that provides emergency grants and subsidies to help income-eligible households in Maryland pay their electricity, gas, and other utility bills. The program assists households facing utility termination or experiencing emergency situations. Grant amounts are determined based on household income, household size following current fiscal year income guidelines, and electric use over the past 12 months. Assistance is available once per program year (July through June). Grants are sent directly to the utility company to help pay past due or ongoing bills, and customers are placed on budget billing plans to spread their annual costs into equal monthly payments. In Montgomery County, grants of up to $2,000 are available toward past due electric utility bills, applied as either a one-time credit or divided into 12 monthly credits. A 55-day hold on electric utility accounts is available if applicants apply within 14 days of termination notice issuance (one hold per program year). Local access points are available statewide, including in Montgomery County through Housing Stabilization Services, in Frederick through the City of Frederick, in Washington County through the Washington County Community Action Council, in St. Mary's County through the Tri-County Community Action Committee at senior activity centers, and in Prince George's County through the Department of Social Services. Application status can be checked online at myohepstatus.maryland.gov. Eligibility is determined by income limits based on household size and gross monthly income.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Financial assistance to help households pay electric, gas, heating, and other utility bills. Grants are sent directly to the utility company to help pay past due or ongoing bills. Grant amounts are determined based on household income, household size following current fiscal year income guidelines, and electric use over the past 12 months. Assistance covers emergency situations and utility termination prevention. Available once per program year (July through June). Customers must enroll in budget billing plans to spread their annual costs into equal monthly payments. In Montgomery County, applicants may receive up to $2,000 towards past due electric utility bills, with the grant applied as a one-time credit to the fuel supplier or divided into 12 monthly credits to reduce monthly payments. A 55-day hold on electric utility accounts is available if applicants apply within 14 days of termination notice issuance (one hold per program year). Eligible customers receive help paying a portion of their current utility bills. St. Mary's County provides annual grants applied directly to electric bills for current or past due bills, with applications accepted between July and May each year. Eligibility is determined by household gross income, with income limits varying by household size and program year. Emergency assistance is available for those facing utility shut off. Available statewide through the Maryland Department of Human Services, with local access points in Montgomery County through Housing Stabilization Services, in Frederick through the City of Frederick, in Washington County through the Washington County Community Action Council, in St. Mary's County through senior activity centers, and in Prince George's County through the Department of Social Services.
