Must be at least 16 years old by the first day of camp to earn college credits
Selected and interviewed by local Forestry Board
Attendance for the entire week required to earn college credits
Must complete an exam to earn college credits
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications are submitted to local Forest Conservancy District Boards or available through the Maryland Forestry Boards website at http://www.marylandforestryboards.org/nrcc.cfm. Each Forestry Board is responsible for recruiting, interviewing, and selecting two students from their counties, and providing partial scholarships.

structured_extraction.program_description: A voucher-based program providing financial assistance to Maryland and Delaware commercial and charter vessels directly or reasonably expected to be impacted by wind turbines in Lease Area OCS-A 0490. The program facilitates safe navigation through equipment installation/upgrades and training for safe navigation and fishing activities around wind turbines. Eligible ocean-going commercial fishing vessels and operators receive equipment upgrades and training such as radar training and vessel navigation equipment upgrades, with up to $10,000 for equipment upgrades on commercial/for-hire fishing vessels, up to $5,000 for charter vessels, and training support up to $1,000 per vessel for multiple participants including radar training and professional mariner certification. An additional $35,000 is available toward experiential training at Maryland Maritime Institute of Technology and Graduate Studies (MITAGS) with fishing vessel-specific wind facility simulation. Participants choose from preferred equipment vendors and training options. The eligible number of vessels and individuals was determined based on coastal fishing industry input.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The NETP provides voucher-based assistance to eligible Maryland and Delaware commercial and charter fishing vessels. Equipment upgrades are funded up to $10,000 for commercial and for-hire fishing vessels and up to $5,000 for charter vessels. Training assistance provides up to $1,000 per vessel for up to two participants for professional mariner certification, radar training, or income loss recovery during training participation. An additional $35,000 is available toward experiential training at Maryland Maritime Institute of Technology and Graduate Studies (MITAGS) with fishing vessel-specific wind facility simulation. Participants can choose from preferred vendors. Funds cannot support litigation, regulatory, or petitioning activities. Unclaimed funds revert to US Wind 5 years after Commercial Operation Date.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Program establishment required 120 days prior to Offshore Construction Commencement Date
structured_extraction.contact_name: Katherine Charbonneau, Assistant Secretary for Aquatic Resources
structured_extraction.program_audience: Commercial and for-hire charter fishers in Maryland and Delaware, vessel owners and individual fishers navigating within and near Lease Area OCS-A 0490 (federal waters off the Delmarva Peninsula), and those reasonably expected to be impacted by offshore wind turbines.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Navigation equipment upgrades and installation for safe navigation around wind turbines, training for safe navigation and fishing activities around wind turbines, professional mariner and radar training, registration fees for training participation, recovery of reasonable income losses for training participation time, and experiential training at MITAGS with wind facility simulation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Maryland and Delaware commercial and charter vessels operating within and near Lease Area OCS-A 0490 in federal waters off the Delmarva Peninsula, approximately 11.5 miles off Ocean City, Maryland. Primarily serves West Ocean City Harbor area in Maryland and associated coastal regions.
requirements_list: Ocean-going commercial fishing captain or vessel owner status
Commercial fishing vessel or U.S. Coast Guard inspected for-hire fishing vessel status
Charter vessel or individual vessel owner and fisher status
Operating within or reasonably expected to be impacted by Lease Area OCS-A 0490 offshore wind project
Eligible vessel and individual count determined based on coastal fishing industry input
Must be operating in or near the offshore wind project area
MDNR approval required for eligibility determination
Funds cannot support litigation, regulatory activities, or petitioning activities
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Voucher-based system administered through Regional Fund Administrator process. Eligibility determined by program administrator. Participants select from preferred vendor list for equipment and training services. Annual reporting required on implementation, including eligibility denials. US Wind provides annual summary reports. Program establishment occurs 120 days prior to Offshore Construction Commencement Date.

structured_extraction.program_description: A permit required for any person engaged in aquaculture or related activities, including pond rearing of fish, tank culture, and other permitted species for human consumption and commercial sale, as well as educational projects. The permit is free of charge and must be renewed every five years.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free permit for operating an aquaculture facility. The permit authorizes non-shellfish aquaculture operations including tank culture, pond culture, and educational projects. Technical assistance is provided for growing methods and aquatic disease control upon request. The permit has a five-year duration and is subject to review and renewal. An annual report is required summarizing activities, production techniques, and the number or amount of finfish or other permitted species stocked or harvested. Quarterly shipping and receiving records must be maintained for three years.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Aquaculture operators including commercial, hobby, research, and educational projects.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Pond rearing, tank culture, and other permitted aquaculture operations for human consumption and commercial sale.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Maryland statewide. Applies to aquacultural activities involving finfish in the tidal waters of the State.
requirements_list: Must apply for and obtain a permit before operating an aquaculture facility
Must renew permit every five years
Must submit an annual report summarizing activities, production techniques, and stocking or harvesting numbers
Health certification and origin documentation for species required
Facility location map with directions required
Description of culture operation and facility sketch required
Location of nearest body of water for discharge must be identified
Solid waste management plan for mortalities and byproducts required
Treatment and entrapment systems for hybrid or non-native species required
Statement of operation goals and expected production required
Workers' compensation insurance certificate required if employing staff
All necessary permits and regulatory compliance required
Quarterly shipping and receiving records must be maintained for 3 years
Immediate notification of disease discovery required
Allow department facility inspections
Notify department of significant modifications
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the Aquaculture Permit Application (both sides) and submit to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources with all required attachments. A facility inspection is required before permit issuance. For renewals and amendments, resubmit the application noting desired changes.

structured_extraction.program_description: A free gear-lending program for active military and their immediate families that provides camping equipment including tents, chairs, stoves, lanterns and more. The program is designed to help military individuals and families new to camping or experienced campers stationed or recovering in Maryland reconnect with each other and the outdoors in a comfortable, safe and relaxing setting. The program also offers an opportunity to experience Maryland's natural, cultural, historical and recreational resources firsthand, including food menus and recipe ideas. Participants can reserve campsites at seven participating state parks: Cunningham Falls State Park, Swallow Falls State Park, New Germany State Park, Rocky Gap State Park, Patapsco Valley State Park, Pocomoke River State Park, and Janes Island State Park, which offer picnic tables, fire pits, electric hook-ups at some sites, and nearby restroom and shower facilities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides a free loan of camping gear (tent, sleeping pads, lantern, chairs, cook stove, roasting sticks) and discounted campsite reservations at participating state parks. Campsites have picnic tables, fire pits, and some sites with electric hook-ups. Restrooms and shower facilities are available nearby.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Active military members and their immediate families, as well as families and individuals interested in camping. No age restrictions for children. Service animals welcome; pets allowed in designated loops.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Camping experience and education using loaned camping gear at state parks
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Programs available at seven participating Maryland state parks: Cunningham Falls State Park, Swallow Falls State Park, New Germany State Park, Rocky Gap State Park, Patapsco Valley State Park, Pocomoke River State Park, and Janes Island State Park. Rocky Gap State Park is located in Allegany County.
requirements_list: Must be active military or immediate family member of active military
Must be stationed or recovering in Maryland area
Must be new to camping or an experienced camper
Must contact the park directly by phone to make a reservation
Must specify 'Operation Campout!' gear reservation when calling
Campsites accommodate up to 6 people
Participants must bring own sleeping bags, food, and personal items
No importation of personal firewood allowed (Emerald Ash Borer threat)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact participating park directly by phone to reserve campsite and gear. Specify 'Operation Campout!' gear reservation when calling. Camping fees still apply.

structured_extraction.program_description: This program helps communities understand and enhance their capacity to plan for impacts from coastal and precipitation-based flood events. It supports planning projects that assess flood risks and vulnerabilities, identify and incorporate adaptation strategies into current planning processes, develop conceptual designs or engineered solutions for identified adaptations, and result in risk-reduction strategies or higher regulatory standards that lead to on-the-ground adaptation projects. The program provides Relative Sea Level Rise (RSLR) estimates and guidance for flood resilience planning based on tide gauge data from multiple locations in Maryland and Delaware, including frameworks for assessing flood risk tolerance and selecting appropriate RSLR estimates for different project timeframes. Particular focus is on tidal flooding, sea level rise, and precipitation-induced flooding.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Projects may receive direct financial support through a grant award or technical assistance through a DNR contractor or Watershed & Climate Services selected provider. Proposal requests typically range from $40,000 to $100,000 for projects with a maximum duration of one year. Maximum request is $125,000. Funding becomes available October 1, 2026. Technical guidance includes RSLR estimates above 2000 levels using RCP 8.5 emissions pathway beyond 2050, categorized by three flood risk tolerance levels (High: 17% probability; Medium: 5% probability/1-in-20 chance; Low: 1% probability/1-in-100 chance). Guidance provides step-by-step framework for planning flood-resilient projects, tools for visualizing current and projected coastal flooding impacts, and recommendations for adaptation strategies (avoidance, resistance, accommodation, relocation).
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: December 12, 2025
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local jurisdictions, non-governmental organizations, and institutions of higher education interested in addressing flood resilience and climate adaptation planning. Coastal communities in Maryland facing tidal flooding and climate change impacts seeking to address flood resilience. Decision-makers and stakeholders planning coastal resilience projects, including municipal and state planners and project developers.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funding supports planning projects that assess flood risks and vulnerabilities, identify and incorporate adaptation strategies into current planning processes, develop conceptual designs or engineered solutions for identified adaptations, and result in risk-reduction strategies or higher regulatory standards that lead to on-the-ground adaptation projects. Community vulnerability assessments and resilience building activities related to tidal, sea level rise, and precipitation-induced flooding.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects must be located within Maryland's Coastal Zone. Since these are planning projects, the project area can encompass both public and private lands. Technical guidance applies to Maryland and Delaware coastal areas with established tide gauge stations, including locations in Annapolis, Baltimore, Cambridge, Lewes (DE), Solomons Island, and Washington DC.
requirements_list: Applicant must be a local jurisdiction, non-governmental organization, or institution of higher education
Projects must be located within Maryland's Coastal Zone
Proposals addressing tidal flooding should reference the jurisdiction's nuisance flood plan, flood mitigation plan, or other planning processes
Proposals addressing sea level rise must use and include completed Appendix A from the Guidance for Using Maryland's 2023 Sea Level Rise Projections
Proposals addressing precipitation-induced flooding should be consistent with trends in the Northeast chapter of the Fourth National Climate Assessment
Project outcomes should result in risk-reduction strategies and higher regulatory standards
Proposals must demonstrate commitment to achieving program change in local programs, policies, or decisions
Applicants must address environmental justice and the needs of historically underserved, overburdened, and BIPOC communities
Proposals must describe significant local need and climate-induced flood impacts
Projects must demonstrate technical and financial feasibility
Proposals must describe climate tools and resources used to develop the proposed approach
Partners must be identified with demonstrated commitment to participate

Required attachments include signed transmittal letter on official letterhead from authorized executive, letters of support from county or town council or appropriate decision-making body, photographs of impacted areas, complete budget table, Appendix A if applicable, and communication and engagement strategy
Use best available RSLR science in decision-making
Prioritize equity and justice principles in planning and adaptation
Incorporate stakeholder perspectives in project development
Consider projects holistically across jurisdictional levels
Support greenhouse gas reduction efforts in adaptation strategies
Protect critical infrastructure and natural/cultural/historic resources
Coordinate across jurisdictional levels
Consider costs and legal liability of adaptation options
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit proposals through the Grants Gateway portal at https://webportalapp.com/sp/login/grants_gateway. Proposals must include all required attachments: transmittal letter, letters of support, photographs, budget table, Appendix A if addressing sea level rise, and communication and engagement strategy. Proposals are reviewed based on completeness, problem and need description, appropriateness of proposed work, use of climate resources and tools, alignment with flood risk reduction goals, advancement of flood risk reduction and adaptation strategies, community and stakeholder engagement, identified partner commitment, and readiness to proceed. Selected proposals receive either direct financial support or technical assistance. Follow six-step approach for RSLR assessment: identify project timeframe and asset inventory, determine flood risk tolerance level, select appropriate tide gauge for project location, select RSLR estimate based on risk tolerance and timeframe, assess flood impacts, and consider adaptation options.

structured_extraction.program_description: A competitive grant program providing matching grants to fund park projects and outdoor recreation facilities in underserved communities. The program is based on Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) rules and regulations and funds acquisition and development of parks and outdoor recreation areas, as well as renovation of existing facilities. Projects must be located in communities with 25,000 or more residents in the 2020 Census and determined to be underserved using environmental justice screening tools such as CEJST, EJScreen, or other written documentation. The National Park Service selects applicants based on pre-applications and requires final applications within one year. The program improves parks, recreational opportunities, and conservation areas in urban and underserved communities, supports public-private partnerships to leverage project support, empowers communities through local public greenspace investment, fosters resilience and sustainable landscape development, restores ecosystems, protects biodiversity, and provides recreational and economic benefits.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Matching grants providing up to 50% of total project-related allowable costs for acquisition of land and development of facilities for public outdoor recreation. 100% assistance available for eligible insular areas (American Samoa, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, U.S. Virgin Islands). Grants typically range from $300,000 to $15,000,000 per award, with 25-40 awards anticipated per calendar year. Eligible projects include community parks, campgrounds, playgrounds, sport fields, trails, water-based recreation, nature preserves, community gardens, amphitheaters, and interpretive signage. Maximum 25% of total budget can be used for costs not directly attributable to physical development/rehabilitation, supplies, equipment, or land acquisition. The program operates on a competitive basis at the federal level, with the National Park Service selecting applicants based on pre-applications and requiring final applications within one year of selection. Applicants submit pre-applications to DNR by the specified deadline, and if approved, submit full applications to the National Park Service.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Semi-annual submission deadlines: June 1 and November 1 of each year (11:59 PM Eastern Time Zone). Dates listed for 2025, 2026, 2027, 2028, 2029. Spring Round: April 15 (pre-applications to DNR), June 1 (full applications to NPS); Fall Round: September 15 (pre-applications to DNR), November 1 (full applications to NPS)
structured_extraction.program_audience: State governments, local governments, non-Federal entities, federally recognized Indian tribes, Alaska Native Corporations and Organizations, Native Hawaiian Communities, public agencies and non-profit organizations in underserved urban communities with populations of 25,000 or more according to the 2020 Census. Also includes U.S. Territories, Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and eligible insular areas.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Land acquisition for parks and recreation areas; new outdoor recreation facility development; renovation and rehabilitation of existing recreation facilities; green infrastructure implementation; ecosystem restoration; disaster resilience measures; planning requirements; park projects in underserved communities; physical connections among recreation areas such as trails and waterways; cultural preservation; native landscape restoration; water resource protection; and active living initiatives.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects must be located in communities with a population of 25,000 or more according to the 2020 Census and determined to be underserved using CEJST, EJScreen, or other written documentation. Also eligible: U.S. Territories, Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, eligible insular areas (American Samoa, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, U.S. Virgin Islands), and tribal lands.
requirements_list: Located in a community with population of 25,000 or more in 2020 Census
Located within a community determined to be underserved (using CEJST, EJScreen, or other written documentation)
Project must comply with Land and Water Conservation Fund rules and regulations
Project must align with state's Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP)
Register in U.S. Treasury's Automated Standard Application for Payments (ASAP) for domestic recipients
Submit Federal Financial reports (SF-425) and Program Performance reports
Infrastructure projects must comply with American iron, steel, manufactured products, and construction materials requirements per 2 CFR 184
Public access guarantee to park or recreation facility site
Provide geospatial software-ready file of encumbered site for LWCF program record meeting Federal Geospatial Data Committee (FGDC) or DOI standards
GIS files must include complete metadata
Monitor award activities and report per 2 CFR 200.329
Perpetual protection requirements apply per LWCF Act
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications occur in two annual rounds: Spring and Fall. Applicants submit pre-applications to DNR by the deadline (April 15 for Spring Round or September 15 for Fall Round) for eligibility and completeness review. If approved, applicants submit full applications to the National Park Service through Grants.gov by the next deadline (June 1 for Spring Round or November 1 for Fall Round), with submissions due by 11:59 PM Eastern Time Zone. The NPS selects applicants and notifies successful applicants about final application requirements within approximately three months. Anticipated project start is one year from selection notification, with project completion anticipated within 1-3 years from date of last Grant Agreement signature. Applicants should contact Molly Pickel or ORLP_Inquiries@nps.gov to discuss potential projects. For technical questions about Grants.gov submissions, contact Grants.gov Customer Support at 1-800-518-4726.

structured_extraction.program_description: The PLANT Award (People Loving and Nurturing Trees) recognizes Maryland communities that plant, care for, and promote trees. Communities of all types can participate, including schools, homeowners associations, parks, local governments, government facilities, scout groups, and faith-based organizations. The program supports communities of all sizes in building urban and community forestry programs through awards at different levels (Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Green) based on activity and effort. Communities recognized through Tree City USA or Tree Campus USA automatically qualify at the Green level.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program recognizes and awards communities at different levels (Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Green) based on their tree planting, care, and promotion activities. Bronze is for single events or one-time efforts such as tree plantings or Arbor Day activities. Silver is for communities beginning to organize such as forming a tree committee or starting an inventory. Gold is for communities actively managing their trees through policies, planning, or coordinated programs. Green is for established programs with sustained effort, dedicated expertise, and ongoing support. Communities recognized through Tree City USA or Tree Campus USA automatically qualify at the Green level.

Authorization to trap peregrine falcons is available in General or Master permit classes.

structured_extraction.program_description: A large-scale, community-based watershed restoration partnership that coordinates forestry efforts to restore and protect the Potomac River watershed. The partnership focuses on sharing watershed knowledge, restoring streamsides and wetlands, promoting land protection and stewardship, reducing wildfire and forest health risks, creating more livable communities, and sustaining partnerships across multiple states and organizations.

Support includes riparian forest buffer establishment, forest stewardship planning, fire risk reduction, and community engagement programs. Implementation results have included creation of riparian forest buffers, forest stewardship plans for private forest land, monitoring sites, and public outreach programs.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Forest stewardship planning, riparian forest buffer creation and maintenance, forest management planning, fire risk reduction, urban forest canopy mapping, backyard buffer planting, and community outreach and education

structured_extraction.program_description: Program Open Space is Maryland's long-term land conservation program that acquires and preserves natural areas, parks, forests, and recreational facilities across the state. The program conserves natural resources and provides outdoor recreation opportunities through land acquisition, conservation easements, and capital improvements. Funding comes from a 0.5% state property transfer tax, the Outdoor Recreation Land Loan of 1969, and federal Land and Water Conservation Fund dollars. POS provides open space areas and community park amenities including parks, forests, wildlife management areas, playgrounds, ball fields, tennis courts, boating facilities, swimming pools, fishing sites, hunting areas, golf courses, hiking trails, greenways, and historic sites. POS has two components: POS Stateside, which funds state park acquisition and development through a Targeting System using scientific information to allocate limited funds, and POS Local, which provides financial and technical assistance to local subdivisions (counties and municipalities) for planning, acquiring, and developing recreation land or open space areas. POS Local is an annual grant program that provides grants to counties and the City of Baltimore for the acquisition of land for conservation and park purposes as well as for the development of public recreation facilities. Funds are allocated annually to the 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City based on a formula, with individual projects determined by local jurisdictions and approved by the Maryland Board of Public Works. Over 6,700 projects have been funded through POS Local to date.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Program Open Space provides funding for land and water conservation, park acquisition, and development of recreational facilities. POS provides funding for land acquisition through fee simple purchases and conservation easements, capital improvements, critical maintenance, and operations in state parks. POS Local provides financial and technical assistance to counties and municipalities for planning, acquisition, and development of recreation land and open space areas. Funds are allocated annually to the 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City based on a formula. Funds may be used to acquire or develop land for public recreation or open space use. Individual projects funded are determined by the local jurisdiction and brought to the Maryland Board of Public Works for approval. POS Stateside projects are driven by a Targeting System using scientific information to allocate limited funds. Annual grants are provided to counties and the City of Baltimore for acquiring land for conservation and parks and for developing public recreation facilities. Assistance includes acquisition grants (reimbursement up to 75-100% of eligible costs), development grants, capital renewal grants, and planning grants (up to $25,000 annually). Reimbursement is provided based on fair market value (average of two independent appraisals) or actual price paid, whichever is less. Eligible costs include land acquisition, contractor services, direct purchases, force account/in-house labor, equipment rental, and incidental costs such as surveys, appraisals, title searches, legal fees, settlement fees, and recording costs. Prepaid taxes refunded to the seller are not eligible. Reimbursement covers contract costs, direct purchases, force account/in-house labor, equipment, and services for community parks and playgrounds projects.

Prepaid taxes refunded to seller are not eligible.

Program Open Space Stateside projects use a Targeting System to guide where limited funds are directed. Program Open Space Local serves all Maryland counties and municipalities. Participation requires an approved Land Preservation, Parks, and Recreation Plan per Section 5-905(b)(2) of the Natural Resources Article of the Maryland Annotated Code. Projects must conform to county Land Preservation and Recreation Plan and be consistent with local comprehensive plans and the Maryland Economic Growth, Resource Protection and Planning Act of 1992. Projects must also be consistent with the Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP).

structured_extraction.program_description: Program Open Space Stateside is a land preservation program established in 1969 that protects natural areas for public recreation and watershed and wildlife protection across Maryland through fee simple and conservation easement acquisitions, including permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements. The program reflects Maryland's long-term commitment to conserving natural resources while providing outdoor recreation opportunities for all citizens. Acquired lands are managed by the Department of Natural Resources as State Parks, Forests, and Wildlife and Fisheries Management Areas to support climate change mitigation and adaptation efforts. Funding typically comes from a 0.5 percent State property transfer tax, which is used to acquire fee simple land, conservation easements, and permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements. Conservation easements are perpetual written legal agreements between landowners and the State of Maryland that acquire permanent interest in land to install or maintain conservation practices protecting water quality and natural resources, tailored to the particular land and landowner situation with conservation values and restrictions detailed in legal documents filed with county land records that apply to current and future landowners permanently.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Funding for Program Open Space comes from a 0.5 percent State property transfer tax. The program acquires land through fee simple purchases and conservation easement acquisitions to expand Maryland's system of protected public lands. Fee simple purchases are managed by DNR as State Parks, Forests, and Wildlife and Fisheries Management Areas. POS Stateside funding is also used for the purchase of permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements, which are perpetual written legal agreements between landowners and the State of Maryland that acquire permanent interest in land to install or maintain conservation practices protecting water quality and natural resources. Conservation easements are tailored to the particular land and landowner situation, with conservation values and restrictions detailed in legal documents filed with county land records that apply to current and future landowners permanently. All lands are managed for climate resilience, recreation, and natural resource protection. For CREP easements, land must be maintained in approved vegetation types per conservation plan, no structures may be built on enrolled lands, and landowners must maintain land in the vegetation type indicated in the conservation plan after federal contracts expire.
structured_extraction.program_audience: The state of Maryland and its citizens through conservation and public recreation opportunities, including landowners and conservation organizations seeking to preserve natural areas in Maryland, and landowners with existing federal CREP or CRP contracts who have installed prescribed conservation practices
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Acquisition of fee simple land and conservation easements for natural area preservation, public recreation, watershed protection, and wildlife protection. Includes purchase of permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements managed as State Parks, Forests, and Wildlife and Fisheries Management Areas. CREP easement funds support installation or maintenance of conservation practices with land maintained in approved vegetation types per conservation plan.

structured_extraction.program_description: A permit that allows the holder to operate a regulated shooting area where captive-raised birds (pheasant, bobwhite quail, chukar partridge, Hungarian partridge, turkeys, and mallard ducks) can be released and shot. The permit is available for both commercial operations (open to the public) and non-commercial operations (closed to the public or with closed membership). The permit authorizes the licensee to raise and release properly marked, captive-raised birds on the designated property, and retriever training may also occur on the premises.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A permit issued upon receipt of an application, a copy of a tax map showing the tract of land to be licensed, proof of workers' compensation insurance compliance, and an annual fee of $150.00. The permit is valid from the date of issuance until the following June 30. The permit allows the licensee to raise and release properly marked, captive-raised birds on the designated property. For free-flying mallard ducks, applications must be received before September 1 annually, and a habitat management plan is required. Minimum property size is 50 acres for hunting flighted mallard ducks and 100 acres for all other species. Retriever training may also occur on the premises. structured_extraction.program_description: A state and federally-funded program supporting implementation of living shorelines and other nature-based restoration projects to help protect communities from erosion, flooding, storm impacts, and climate change. The program provides financial and technical assistance for projects that provide benefits to a community, municipality, or county through design, permitting, construction, and adaptive management of shoreline restoration or stormwater projects. Projects use nature-based restoration techniques such as living shorelines, wetland restoration, dune restoration, beneficial use of dredged material, and green stormwater practices. Grants typically between $30,000 and $100,000 are provided for design and permitting of restoration projects. Funding is provided by the State of Maryland and the National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration. For the CY2026/FY2027 grant cycle, only design and permitting proposals are eligible; construction projects are not funded at this time due to funding limitations. Design and permit projects typically must be completed within 24 months. Funding will be available July 1, 2026 through October 1, 2026 depending on fund source and state/federal approvals.

Technical assistance and guidance are provided for evaluation, design, maintenance, and monitoring of restoration projects. Permitting fees are not eligible. Community public property is prioritized, and funding on private residential properties can be difficult to obtain. structured_extraction.program_name: Roots for Resilience: Living Shoreline Projects
structured_extraction.program_description: A Maryland Department of Natural Resources initiative funded through the EPA's Climate Pollution Reduction Grant (CPRG) supporting climate resilience through living shoreline restoration, tree planting, coastal habitat restoration, and community engagement. The program solicits applications for construction, design/build, and design proposals for large-scale living shoreline projects and other nature-based solutions that enhance coastal resilience, protect tidal marsh habitat, and strengthen natural defenses against erosion, flooding, and storm impacts while reducing carbon emissions. Living shorelines are nature-based coastal structures using erosion control techniques such as fiber coir logs, sills, groins, breakwaters, natural materials, and marsh plantings to protect wetlands and reduce erosion while providing climate resilience benefits. Projects are supported on Maryland's Lower Eastern Shore (Dorchester, Somerset, and Wicomico Counties in Chesapeake Bay portions), with particular focus on initiatives that collectively protect substantial areas of high-quality tidal marsh habitat in the Chesapeake Bay region and enhance nature's ability to store carbon. The program aims to award projects that collectively protect a total of 400 acres of adjacent high-quality tidal marsh habitat. Projects must provide community-wide coastal protection benefits through nature-based approaches and consider climate change data to address future conditions.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive 100% federal grant funding (no match required, though leveraged funding is viewed favorably). Minimum request of $1 million; smaller design-only requests may be allowed with DNR approval. Total funding available: $17 million. Grants awarded to support living shoreline restoration, tree planting, coastal habitat restoration, and community engagement projects. Funding supports construction, design/build, and design services for shoreline restoration and nature-based climate resilience initiatives. Provides funding for design, permitting, construction, and adaptive management of shoreline restoration or stormwater projects that address flooding and/or erosion. Eligible costs include engineering/technical services, permits, community engagement, contractor/consultant services, native plants and materials, staff time, monitoring, indirect costs, and outreach activities. Permitting fees are not eligible as a standalone cost. Funding is available for each phase of project development. Large-scale projects in Dorchester, Somerset, or Wicomico Counties that collectively protect substantial areas of adjacent high-quality tidal marsh habitat (goal of 400 acres total) and enhance community resilience to erosion, flooding, and storm impacts are prioritized. The program funds construction, design and build, design work, tree planting initiatives, coastal habitat restoration, and community engagement activities through a Request for Proposals process.

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland's Rural Legacy Program is a state-funded program created by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources in 1998 that preserves large blocks of working rural lands and protects Maryland's best natural, agricultural, historical, and cultural areas by preserving large, contiguous tracts of land and enhancing natural resource, agricultural, forestry, and environmental protection while supporting a sustainable land base for natural resource-based industries. The program currently includes 36 designated Rural Legacy Areas throughout the state. It encourages local governments and private land trusts to identify Rural Legacy Areas—delineated areas within a county that include both working farms and ecologically significant landscapes—and apply for grant funds to purchase conservation easements from willing landowners, acquire land, or complement existing land conservation efforts. Through this program, landowners can sell or donate their development rights, which are permanently extinguished, while retaining ownership of their land to continue farming or raising livestock. The program helps establish and maintain Rural Legacy Areas through land acquisition and planning, allowing groups to propose new Rural Legacy Areas or request grant renewals and boundary changes for already established areas. Grants are awarded to Rural Legacy Area Sponsors for land acquisition, conservation, and planning purposes. Protection is achieved through acquiring easements and fee simple estates from willing landowners. The program emphasizes stream buffer protection, requiring 100 foot grass and/or forest buffers as part of the resource protection element. Once the Board of Public Works approves an application, a Grant Agreement is executed between the Rural Legacy Board and the Sponsor, allowing the sponsor to proceed with individual land acquisitions. The program uses an objective scoring approach to review and allocate its limited grant funds. Applications are evaluated based on the significance of agricultural, forestry, natural and cultural resources; threat from development pressure; historic and cultural resource significance; economic value of resource-based industries and services; application quality and completeness; partnership strength; matching funds provided; and sponsor capacity. Since 1997, the program has awarded over $403.5 million. The program establishes greenbelts of forests and farms around rural communities to preserve cultural heritage and sense of place, preserves critical habitat for native plants and wildlife species, and protects riparian forests, wetlands, and greenways to buffer the Chesapeake Bay from pollution runoff.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grant funding awarded through a formal application and approval process to purchase conservation easements from willing landowners in designated Rural Legacy Areas or to provide cash payments for the sale of development rights at settlement. Annual grants are awarded to Rural Legacy Area Sponsors and to local governments and private land trusts for land acquisition, planning, conservation, and establishment and maintenance of Rural Legacy Areas. Funding allocation uses an objective scoring approach. Easements protect agricultural, natural, historical, cultural resources, and stream buffers, and remain effective in perpetuity. The program requires 100 foot grass and/or forest buffers as part of the resource protection element. Landowners can sell or donate their development rights while retaining ownership to continue farming or raising livestock. Proceeds from the sale of conservation easements provide financial compensation to landowners. Funding is provided by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and comes from Maryland Program Open Space dollars and general obligation bonds from the state capital budget for preservation of large, contiguous land tracts and enhancement of natural resources and agricultural, forestry, and environmental protection. Once the Board of Public Works approves an application, a Grant Agreement is executed between the Rural Legacy Board and the Sponsor. Funds are encumbered following Board of Public Works approval, typically in August or September. Applications are evaluated based on resource significance, development threat, historic and cultural resource value, economic value of protected industries, application quality, partnership strength, matching funds provided, sponsor capacity, property size, number of development rights, proximity to other permanent easements, agricultural characteristics, historic characteristics, and environmental characteristics. Conservation easements must include soil conservation and water quality plans, forest management plans, and may include 100-foot riparian buffers to qualify for additional scoring points. Administrative costs may comprise up to 3% of grant amount. Stewardship and monitoring expenses are eligible, as are incidental costs such as surveys, appraisals, title searches, and settlement costs.

Specific areas include Washington County locations surrounding the Towns of Sharpsburg, Keedysville, Boonsboro and the Rural Villages of St. James, Lappans, Fairplay, Rohrersville and Gapland, as well as Anne Arundel County and other eligible counties throughout Maryland. Properties in vicinity of or ecologically related to military installations (when Navy is co-grantee).

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Local governments and private land trusts identify Rural Legacy Areas and apply annually to the Rural Legacy Board for participation and funding. Qualifying landowners and Rural Legacy Area Sponsors submit applications by the second Tuesday in February by 5:00 p.m. or prior to February 1st or December 1st depending on the local jurisdiction cycle. Groups interested in establishing a new Rural Legacy Area should read the Rural Legacy Program Grants Manual and meet with the RLP Program Administrator. For new areas, complete a Full Application. For established areas, use the Abbreviated Application form and Property List Form. All applications must follow GIS Submittal Guidelines. After completion, contact your program administrator. Applications are reviewed and ranked based on property size, number of development rights, proximity to other permanent easements, agricultural characteristics, historic characteristics, and environmental characteristics using an objective scoring approach. Applicants submit either a Full Application for new Rural Legacy Areas or an Abbreviated Application for grant renewals and boundary expansions of existing Rural Legacy Areas. Applications must include GIS data according to submittal guidelines. Property lists and conservation easement documents are required as part of the application. Complete Cover Sheet with sponsor information and all attachments required. Applications are submitted to the Rural Legacy Office by the second Tuesday in February. Submit electronically in Word or PDF format to Katrina L. Tucker. State agencies review applications from February through April. The Rural Legacy Advisory Committee reviews applications and makes recommendations to the Rural Legacy Board from April through May, conducting site visits as needed and may requesting presentations. The Advisory Committee submits recommendations in June or July. The Rural Legacy Board reviews recommendations and submits final recommendations to the Board of Public Works in July or August. The Board of Public Works designates the Rural Legacy Areas, approves grants in August or September, and recommends to the Governor which areas will be designated and funded. Once the Board of Public Works approves the application, a Grant Agreement is transmitted to the Sponsor for execution. Grant Agreements are prepared from September through October. Funds are contingent on approval by the County Executive and County Council during the Capital Budget cycle. Landowner interest is the basis for requesting County funds each year during the Capital Budget cycle. Final BPW package submission requires legal description of property with surveyor letter or completed survey, conservation easement deed, title policy, settlement sheet, Project Agreement form, and Request for Payment form. Sponsor receives funds and proceeds to settlement after BPW approval. Grantors submit written request with supporting documentation to grantees for approvals. Grantees have 90 days to respond (non-response = constructive denial). Both grantees must approve requests. For utilities/roadways: additional public interest considerations apply.

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland's Rural Legacy Program is a state-funded land conservation program that protects Maryland's best natural, agricultural, historical, and cultural areas by acquiring conservation easements and fee simple estates from willing landowners. The program preserves large blocks of working rural lands for future generations statewide through 36 designated Rural Legacy Areas. It encourages local governments and private land trusts to identify Rural Legacy Areas and apply for funds to purchase development rights, protecting large contiguous tracts of land vulnerable to sprawl development. Landowners can sell or donate their development rights while retaining ownership to continue farming or raising livestock. Protection is achieved through cooperative efforts among state and local governments and land trusts, with easements remaining effective in perpetuity. The program evaluates applications based on the significance of agricultural, forestry, natural and cultural resources; threat from development pressure; historic and cultural resource significance; and economic value of resource-based industries and services such as agriculture, forestry, tourism, and recreation. Groups can propose new Rural Legacy Areas or request grant renewals and boundary changes for already established areas. Since 1997, the program has awarded over $403.5 million. Funding supports preservation of large, contiguous tracts of land and enhancement of natural resource, agricultural, forestry and environmental protection while supporting a sustainable land base for natural resource-based industries. Annual grants are awarded to local sponsors for land acquisition and planning in designated Rural Legacy Areas. The program establishes greenbelts of forests and farms around rural communities to preserve cultural heritage and sense of place, preserves critical habitat for native plants and wildlife species, and protects riparian forests, wetlands, and greenways to buffer the Chesapeake Bay from pollution runoff.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Acquisition of easements and fee simple estates from willing landowners for land conservation and protection of natural and cultural resources, farms, forests, and other open space. Funds support land acquisition and conservation planning to preserve resource-based industries and services such as agriculture, forestry, tourism, and recreation. Acquisition of agricultural, forest, natural, and cultural land through conservation easements and fee simple purchases that permanently restrict development rights while allowing continued agricultural use, forestry, and limited residential structures as permitted by individual easement terms. Preservation of large contiguous tracts of land for natural resource, agricultural, and forestry protection. Land acquisition and conservation in designated Rural Legacy Areas. Incidental costs including surveys, appraisals, title searches, legal fees, and settlement costs. Administrative staff salaries and support. Easement monitoring and stewardship endowments. Environmental assessments. Enhanced best management practices beyond standard practices. Local food supply and farm-to-school programs. Innovative programs for underserved communities.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Local Sponsors submit annual applications to the Rural Legacy Board by the second Tuesday in February by 5:00 p.m. Groups interested in establishing a new Rural Legacy Area should read the Rural Legacy Program Grants Manual and meet with the RLP Program Administrator to discuss the process. For new areas, complete a Full Application. For established areas, use the Abbreviated Application form and Property List Form. All applications must follow GIS Submittal Guidelines and submit a Rural Legacy Plan application. Applicants submit either a Full Application for new Rural Legacy Areas or an Abbreviated Application for grant renewals and boundary expansions of existing Rural Legacy Areas. Applications must include GIS data according to submittal guidelines. Property lists and conservation easement documents are required as part of the application. Complete Cover Sheet with sponsor information and all attachments required. Applications are submitted to the Rural Legacy Office by the second Tuesday in February. Submit electronically in Word or PDF format to Katrina L. Tucker. State agencies review applications from February through April. The Rural Legacy Advisory Committee reviews applications and makes recommendations to the Rural Legacy Board. Applications are evaluated based on resource significance, development threat, historic and cultural resource value, economic value of protected industries, application quality, partnership strength, matching funds provided, and sponsor capacity. The Rural Legacy Advisory Committee and Board review applications from April through May, conduct site visits as needed, and may request presentations. The Advisory Committee submits recommendations in June or July. The Rural Legacy Board reviews applications annually and recommendations to the Governor and Board of Public Works. The Board of Public Works reviews recommendations and approves designations and grants in August or September. Applications are ranked based on property size, number of development rights, proximity to other permanent easements, agricultural characteristics, historic characteristics, and environmental characteristics. Scoring considers county priorities: 2.5 points for first priority area; Baltimore County awards 2.5 points to top two priority areas. After Board of Public Works approval, the Rural Legacy Board transmits a Grant Agreement to the sponsor for signatures. Grant Agreements are prepared from September through October. Once executed, the sponsor can proceed with individual acquisitions. Eligible organizations should contact DNR for additional application details. Local governments and private land trusts identify areas and submit competitive applications which are ranked based on established evaluation criteria. Final BPW package submission requires legal description of property with surveyor letter or completed survey, conservation easement deed, title policy, settlement sheet, Project Agreement form, and Request for Payment form. Sponsor receives funds and proceeds to settlement after BPW approval.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Schoolyard Forests Program is a Five Million Trees partnership initiative with the Maryland Association of Environmental & Outdoor Education that helps Maryland schools create outdoor spaces supporting student well-being and environmental stewardship. The program promotes healthier campus landscapes with nature access for students of all backgrounds and develops partnerships with municipalities, schools, and students to increase tree canopy cover, create nature discovery pathways, and support climate resiliency. Schools may receive campus planning and technical support to identify opportunities for improving outdoor spaces and introducing native plantings, hands-on assistance and training for facilities teams and staff for long-term stewardship, educational and student-centered opportunities that integrate outdoor learning such as campus mapping and nature-based activities, engagement and celebration events like Earth Month and Arbor Day programs, youth career exploration through demonstrations introducing students to natural resource stewardship and green career pathways, and microgrants and classroom support materials for schools advancing toward Green School certification or developing outdoor projects.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Schools receive campus planning and technical support to identify opportunities for improving outdoor spaces and introducing native plantings. Hands-on assistance and training is available for facilities teams, teachers, and staff to build skills in long-term stewardship. Educational and student-centered opportunities integrate outdoor learning into the school day through activities like campus mapping, nature-based activities, and seed collection. Services provided include teacher workshops, landscape stewardship manuals, specimen tree inventory and mapping, forest health assessments, professional development and continuing education, hazard tree evaluation and removal, native tree planting, edible food plots, and summer tree maintenance. Engagement and celebration events like Earth Month and Arbor Day programs foster community involvement. Youth career exploration demonstrates green career pathways. Microgrants and classroom support materials are available for schools advancing toward Green School certification or developing outdoor projects. All services are provided free to eligible schools.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland public schools of all types and sizes, with priority given to schools and communities with the greatest need. Students of all backgrounds are welcome. District-level facility teams and community partners working directly with school campuses are also welcome. Privately funded schools may participate, though program resources are first directed toward public schools.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Schools may use support to strengthen outdoor learning, enhance existing green spaces and tree care, address campus heat and comfort, increase tree canopy cover, create nature discovery pathways, support climate resiliency, plant new trees, introduce native plantings, and develop outdoor projects. Support can be applied to campus planning, stewardship training, educational programming, community events, youth career exploration, and outdoor project development.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to Maryland public schools of all types and sizes statewide, with priority given to schools and communities with the greatest need.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: A formal application process is being developed and will be linked from the program page. In the interim, schools may contact the program administrator directly to discuss interest and initial questions. Schools may also apply online using the Submittable link provided at marylandforestservice.submittable.com.

structured_extraction.program_description: A permit required for properly accredited persons of known scientific attainment to collect wildlife, nests, or eggs from the wild for scientific or educational purposes. The permit also authorizes capturing, marking, and releasing wildlife, as well as salvaging wildlife and maintaining specimens for educational purposes by public educational institutions. The permit is valid through December 31 of the issuing year, and an annual report must be filed by that deadline; failure to submit may result in revocation of existing permits or rejection of future applications. A federal permit from the United States Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS) and/or United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) may be required to collect and/or possess migratory birds or federally listed species.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The permit is issued as authorization to conduct scientific collection activities. The permit is valid through December 31 of the issuing year and authorizes the holder to collect wildlife, nests, eggs, or to capture, mark, and release wildlife for scientific or educational purposes. An annual report must be filed by December 31 of the issuing year; failure to submit may result in revocation of existing permits or rejection of future applications. The permit fee is $10, payable to the Department of Natural Resources. A federal permit from the United States Fish & Wildlife Service or United States Department of Agriculture may also be required for migratory birds or federally listed species.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: No specific deadline; permits expire December 31st following issuance

structured_extraction.program_description: An educational and recreational program for senior citizens designed to get them active, visit local state parks, and connect with nature. Participants attend six weekly sessions led by rangers, historians, naturalists, and Department of Natural Resources experts covering topics such as plants, animals, conservation, history, stewardship, birding, outdoor skills, wellness activities, and nature education. Sessions include exercise, expert-led talks, fellowship, games, hikes, yoga, paddle trips, canoe/kayak trips, historic tours, tree planting, and a statewide gathering. Participants who complete the program become certified Senior Rangers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free or low-cost participation in six weekly instructional sessions at state parks. Sessions run for five to six weeks at various times throughout the year at participating locations including Seneca Creek State Park, Bohemia River State Park, Elk Neck State Park, Patapsco Valley State Park, Southern Maryland Recreational Complex, Tuckahoe State Park complex, Martinak State Park, Sassafrass State Park, Wye Island State Park, and Janes Island State Park. Sessions typically meet either mornings or afternoons for 1.5 to 2 hours per week. Program fee of $40 applies at some locations ($30 for Golden Age Passholders; $10 discount for Golden Age Passholders at other locations). No experience or equipment needed for paddling activities.

Statewide gathering held at Seneca Creek State Park on June 17.

structured_extraction.program_name: Shoreline Erosion Control Revolving Loan Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A revolving loan fund that provides zero-percent interest loans and technical assistance to waterfront property owners, non-profit organizations, community organizations, counties and municipalities experiencing shoreline and streambank erosion along the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries. The program finances living shoreline projects and other nature-based erosion control methods with loan terms ranging from 5 to 20 years depending on the techniques implemented and their associated costs and projected longevity. Technical and financial assistance is provided for design, construction, installation, and materials for shoreline stabilization and streambank restoration projects that protect property from erosion while maintaining natural coastal processes and protecting or creating natural habitat.
list_of_relevant_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Zero percent interest loans ranging from 5 to 20 years depending on techniques implemented and their associated costs and projected longevity. Each loan includes an administrative fee ranging from 3% to 10% based on project construction cost. An upfront cash contribution is required for individuals and groups of homeowners for loans greater than $60,000. Funds are dispersed for portions of completed work with the applicant providing proof of payment to the department. Loans are available for design, construction, materials, and installation. A county-sponsored shore erosion control tax district (for community projects) or a shore erosion control lien (for private property projects) must be established.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Design, construction, installation, and materials for living shorelines and erosion control projects that protect shorelines and streambanks from erosion while maintaining natural coastal processes and protecting or creating natural habitat. Projects may incorporate techniques such as breakwaters, sills, groins, biologs, native marsh grass plantings, and sand. Projects must be living shorelines, not hard structures like bulkheads or riprap.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide along the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries in Maryland and other waterfront properties. A county-sponsored shore erosion control tax district or shore erosion control lien must be established.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through MD DNR Grants Gateway at http://mddnr.info/grantsgateway or fill out a technical assistance request form. Interested property owners should contact Wesley Gould at 410-260-8812 to discuss technical assistance and funding opportunities. The department will assist with establishing the required tax district or lien. Funds are dispersed for portions of completed work, and the applicant must provide proof of payment to the department.

structured_extraction.program_name: Solar Generation Facilities - Pollinator-Friendly Designation Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A certification program that designates commercial ground-mounted solar facilities greater than 1 acre as pollinator-friendly when they implement approved habitat management practices. Solar developers can earn this designation by submitting an application with facility information and a pollinator habitat management plan, using appropriate seed mixes for their Maryland region, undergoing site inspection by a DNR-approved inspector, and maintaining the habitat according to the approved plan. Upon approval, the certification is valid for two years and can be renewed by contacting the program within 90 days of expiration.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides certification and recognition for solar facilities that meet pollinator-friendly standards. Developers submit an application with facility information and a pollinator habitat management plan, work with a DNR-approved site inspector to implement the plan using approved seed mixes appropriate for their Maryland region, and submit a final scorecard and inspector letter. Upon approval, the facility receives a pollinator-friendly certification valid for two years, which can be renewed by contacting the program within 90 days of expiration.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: The program does not provide direct financial assistance or funding. It certifies facilities that implement pollinator habitat management on solar sites and offers technical review services to recognize solar facilities that implement pollinator-friendly habitat management practices.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland for commercial ground-mounted solar facilities of at least 1 acre. All Maryland counties are eligible. Developers should use seed mixes appropriate for their Maryland region.

structured_extraction.program_name: Special Rivers Chesapeake Bay Implementation Grant
structured_extraction.program_description: A program funded since 1983 by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to improve water quality for the Chesapeake Bay by encouraging the restoration, enhancement, and management of forests. The project helps implement Chesapeake Bay Agreement goals including riparian forest buffer restoration, watershed planning, stream corridor restoration, land conservation, stewardship, and community engagement.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides funding for riparian forest buffer restoration and maintenance (at least 30 miles per year), forest stewardship planning for private and public forests (at least 1,800 acres per year), and education and outreach on forest benefits for watersheds and water quality (at least 600 people per year). Since 1983, the project has created over 5,580 acres of forest buffers, prepared forest stewardship plans for over 53,000 acres, and reached over 45,000 people.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Landowners, students, natural resource professionals, and residents of Chesapeake Bay watershed areas in the four project regions: Susquehanna area, Monocacy area, Anacostia/West Chesapeake, and Town Creek
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Riparian forest buffer restoration and monitoring, forest stewardship planning, stream corridor restoration, afforestation, education and outreach programs, professional training, and invasive species control
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Four project areas: (1) Susquehanna area from Elk River in Cecil County to upper and middle Patuxent watersheds in Howard and Montgomery County, including Deer Creek, Bush River, Gunpowder, Jones Falls, Gwynns Falls, and Patapsco watersheds in Baltimore, Carroll, and Harford Counties; (2) Monocacy area covering 1,300 square miles in Upper and Lower Monocacy, Double Pipe, Catoctin, Antietam, Conococheague, Licking Creek and adjacent drainages to the Potomac River; (3) Anacostia/West Chesapeake serving portions of Prince George's, Montgomery, and Anne Arundel Counties; (4) Town Creek watershed in Allegany County, Maryland and Bedford County, Pennsylvania

The waiver applies to the military identification card holder only, and no other facility service charges are waived.

structured_extraction.program_name: State Park Day-Use Area Admission Fee Waiver for Veterans and Active Duty Military
structured_extraction.program_description: A waiver that eliminates all applicable day-use entrance charges to Maryland state parks for veterans of the United States Armed Forces, active duty military personnel, and members of the Maryland National Guard. The waiver provides year-round free day-use entry to state parks for eligible individuals. Both resident and out-of-state veterans are eligible. The waiver applies to the individual displaying proof of eligibility only, though per-vehicle charges are also waived when applicable. No other facility use service charges are waived.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Day-use entrance service charges at Maryland state parks are waived year-round for eligible veterans, active duty military personnel, and Maryland National Guard members. The waiver applies to the individual displaying valid proof of eligibility only and not others in the same vehicle, unless a per-vehicle charge is in effect at the time, in which case the per-vehicle fee is waived. No other facility use service charges are waived.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Day-use admission to Maryland state parks
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide at all Maryland state park day-use areas

structured_extraction.program_description: Grants and loans that support capital projects and services for the boating public, including constructing or renovating boating access facilities, dredging high-use channels and harbors, and purchasing fire and rescue vessels. The program also supports services like ice breaking, navigation aids, derelict boat removal, the Clean Marina Initiative, marine sewage pumpout programs, shore erosion control, and boating safety. Established in 1966 under Annotated Code of Maryland Sec. 8-707 of the State Boat Act, the program funds projects that improve and promote recreational and commercial capabilities, conditions, and safety of Maryland's waterways for benefit of the general boating public. Funding comes primarily from a 5% excise tax on boat purchases and titling in Maryland. Since 1966, the fund has distributed more than $429 million for over 4,900 projects at more than 400 public boating access sites. The program includes specialized grant tracks: the Matching Fund Fire & Rescue Grant (up to $80,000 for marine facilities and equipment for firefighting, police, and medical services); the 25K Off-Cycle WIF Grant (up to $25,000 for small projects at public boating facilities); 100% Local Government Grants (up to $500,000); 100% State Grants for specific projects; Dredging Grants at 100% or with 50/50 Match; Matching Fund Grants (50/50 cost share); and Tax District Dredging Loans (interest-free, up to 25 years).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The Waterway Improvement Fund provides financial support in the form of grants, interest-free long-term loans (up to 25 years for Tax Districts), and reimbursement basis assistance to local governments, the DNR, federal agencies, and authorized volunteer fire departments for a wide variety of capital projects and services for the boating public. Specific funding mechanisms include: (1) 100% Local Government Grants (up to $500,000); (2) 100% State Grants for specific projects; (3) Dredging Grants at 100% or with 50/50 Match; (4) Matching Fund Grants (50/50 cost share); (5) Matching Fund Fire & Rescue Grants with state cost share up to $80,000 (matching fund requiring recipient cost share) for construction of marine facilities for firefighting, police, or medical services; acquisition of vessels and equipment for marine services; and communication equipment for safety and boating public service; (6) Tax District Dredging Loans (interest-free, up to 25 years); (7) Small Project Grants not to exceed $25,000 for minor construction, repair, and navigation improvements at public boating facilities with a one-year performance period (July 1 – June 30); and (8) Reimbursement basis assistance for waterway improvement projects, vessel purchases, in-house labor, and equipment costs. Funding comes primarily from a 5% excise tax on boat purchases and titling in Maryland. Since 1966, the fund has distributed more than $429 million for over 4,900 projects at more than 400 public boating access sites.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Applications typically submitted between July and September for the following fiscal year funding consideration; Small Project Grants can be submitted anytime throughout the fiscal year; funds become available July 1st of each fiscal year
structured_extraction.contact_name: Carla Fleming (overall Center for Waterway Improvement & Infrastructure); Jennifer Jackson (Anne Arundel, Calvert, Charles, Prince George's, St. Mary's); Matt Negley (Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, Somerset, Talbot, Wicomico, Worcester); Jillian Seagraves (Allegany, Baltimore City and County, Carroll, Cecil, Frederick, Garrett, Harford, Howard, Montgomery, Washington); Isaac Wilding (statewide dredging)
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local government jurisdictions (county, town, and city governments), public authorities, federal agencies, and authorized volunteer fire departments and emergency response organizations in Maryland that manage boating facilities and services, as well as the general boating public.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funds can be used to construct, renovate, or maintain boating access facilities; dredge channels and harbors; construct jetties and breakwaters; mark channels and harbors; provide aids to navigation; clear debris and obstructions from navigable waters; manage dredging material placement (DMP) and beneficial use sites; purchase fire and rescue vessels in partnership with local fire companies; support ice breaking and navigation aids; remove derelict boats and debris; manage the Clean Marina Initiative; operate marine sewage pumpout programs; support shore erosion control; provide boating safety services; construct marine facilities for firefighting, police, or medical services; acquire vessels and equipment for marine firefighting, police, and medical services; acquire communication equipment for safety and boating public service; and conduct planning, engineering, construction, and inspection phases of waterway improvement projects.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide to all Maryland counties and public jurisdictions. Program serves all waters of the State of Maryland. Staff contacts are organized by county for application support.
